title: What a backend actually is

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: A phone app or a web page runs on a machine you do not control. The user can edit the page, replay requests, or write their own client. Yet some things must be the same for everyone: your account balance, the order of messages in a chat, whether a username is taken. Those need one place that every client agrees on and that no client can tamper with. That place is the backend. A backend exists because shared truth and trusted rules cannot live on devices you do not own.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The request-response model Two roles. A client starts a conversation by sending a request. A server listens, does some work, and sends back one response. The server never calls the client uninvited in this basic model; it only answers. Everything in this course is some detail of those two arrows: how the client finds the server, how the bytes travel, how the server decides what to do, where it keeps data, and what happens when something fails. A server is a program that does not exit A script runs, prints, and ends. A server starts, binds to a port, and then waits forever for work. Here is the smallest honest backend in Node: Run it and call it twice with curl localhost:3000. The counter survives between requests because the process stays alive. That is also its weakness: restart it and the state is gone. Chapters on databases exist because of that sentence. What a backend owns Shared state. The one copy of the data that all clients agree on.Rules. Who may do what, which values are valid, what must happen together or not at all.Trust. A client can claim anything. The backend checks. A client may show a discount; only the backend may grant one. A client may hide a button; only the backend may refuse the action. Application, framework, runtime The application is the code you wrote: your routes and rules.The framework (Express, Fastify, Nest) parses requests, matches routes and runs middleware, so you do not hand-roll it.The runtime (Node.js) runs your JavaScript and gives it access to sockets, files and timers through the operating system. The next lessons peel those layers: networking underneath, then the protocol, then the machinery around your code.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Trusting the client. Validating a form in the browser improves the user experience, but it protects nothing. Every rule that matters must be enforced again on the server, because requests can be made without your page at all. Keeping important state only in memory. It vanishes on restart and is not shared between two copies of the server.Writing the server like a script, with top-level work that blocks or exits on the first error.Learning one framework instead of the model. Frameworks change every few years; the request-response model has not.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Putting logic on the server makes it trustworthy and consistent, but every action now costs a network round trip and the server becomes a shared resource that can be overloaded or go down. Good designs put presentation on the client and anything that must be true on the server.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: A real backend is never one process on one machine. It runs as several copies behind a load balancer, restarts on failure, keeps state in a database, and is watched with logs and metrics. The mental model stays the same; each of those pieces is a chapter of this course. Because several copies run at once, the visits counter above would be wrong in production: each copy would count its own. That is the first example of a theme you will meet repeatedly: state must live somewhere all copies share.

title: Anatomy of a request

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Every later chapter zooms into one stage of a single journey. Without the map you learn facts that do not connect: DNS here, indexes there. This lesson draws the map once, so each new topic has a place to land. Performance and failures are almost always located in one particular stage. Knowing the stages is how you stop guessing which one.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The journey You click a link to https://api.nexora.dev/users/42. In order: Resolve the name. DNS turns api.nexora.dev into an IP address. See Names, addresses and ports.Open a connection. TCP's handshake costs a round trip. See TCP and the cost of a connection.Secure it. TLS agrees on keys and checks the server's certificate. See TLS.Send the HTTP request. Method, path, headers. See HTTP as text on a socket.Run your code. Middleware, routing, validation, your handler.Fetch state. Often a cache, then a database.Send the response back over the same connection. What is paid once and what is paid every time Stages 1 to 3 belong to the connection. If the browser keeps the connection open and reuses it, a second request skips them. Stages 4 to 7 belong to the request and are paid every time. Try it above: switch the connection to Keep-alive and the DNS cache to Warm, and watch the total fall. Where the time usually goes Distance sets a floor. A round trip to a server 8,000 km away takes at least about 55 ms in fibre (light travels roughly two thirds of its vacuum speed), whatever your code does. A cold HTTPS request can need several of them. After that, the typical order of cost is: database work, then network, then your own code, though it varies. Trust boundaries along the way Everything left of your server is outside your control: the client, the network, even the headers. Everything you do first inside the server should treat input as untrusted. That boundary is why validation (chapter A5) and authentication (chapter A4) sit at the edge of your code.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Optimising code before measuring. Teams spend days speeding up a handler that accounts for 3 ms of a 400 ms request, while a missing keep-alive or an uncached lookup costs far more. Ignoring distance. Putting the server in one region and users in another adds round trips you cannot optimise away in code.Treating the database as free. One request that makes ten sequential queries pays ten round trips to the database.Forgetting the first request is special. Load tests that reuse one connection hide the handshake cost real users pay.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Each stage you remove or shorten (caching, connection reuse, edge servers) buys speed at the price of staleness, complexity or cost. A cache makes reads fast and makes data possibly out of date. Choose which stage to shorten based on a measurement, not a habit.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Teams record timing per stage: DNS, connect, TLS, time to first byte, total. When a page feels slow, the breakdown tells you which stage to investigate. Browser developer tools show the same breakdown for any request in the Network tab (the Timing view). Percentiles matter more than averages. If 1 request in 100 takes ten times longer, the average barely moves, but a user who makes twenty requests per page will often hit one of the slow ones.

title: Names, addresses and ports

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Machines route packets by number. People remember words. Everything in this chapter exists to bridge those two facts: a name that humans type, an IP address that routers understand, and a port that picks one program out of everything running on that machine. Without ports, a machine with one IP address could run exactly one network program. Without DNS, every address change would break every bookmark on earth.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Three identifiers, three jobs An IP address identifies a network interface, for example 93.184.216.34 for IPv4 or 2606:2800:220:1:: for IPv6. A port is a 16-bit number (0 to 65535) that identifies one program listening on that interface. The pair (IP, port) is an endpoint. A TCP connection is identified by four values: source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port. That four-tuple is what the operating system uses to hand incoming bytes to the right process. Your browser does not choose port 443 for itself. It connects to 443 on the server, and the OS silently picks a free ephemeral source port, usually somewhere above 32768, for its own end. Resolving a name When you type api.example.com, a library asks a recursive resolver (usually run by your ISP, your company or a public provider) for its address. If the resolver has no fresh cached answer, it walks the hierarchy: Ask a root server: "who handles .com?" It replies with the TLD servers.Ask a TLD server: "who handles example.com?" It replies with the domain's authoritative servers.Ask the authoritative server: "what is the A record for api.example.com?" It replies with an IP and a TTL. The resolver caches the answer for TTL seconds and returns it to you. The next asker inside that window never leaves the resolver. In Node.js Node gives you two different doors, and they behave differently: dns.lookup is what fetch and net.connect use. It runs in libuv's thread pool, so a burst of slow lookups can queue behind each other and starve other pool work such as file I/O. dns.resolve4 uses a real DNS client (c-ares) and does not.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Treating a TTL as a promise. It is an upper bound on how long a well-behaved cache may keep an answer. Some resolvers and some JVM and OS settings cache longer, so a DNS change is never instantly global. Hardcoding IPs for a service you do not control. The address will change, and the failure will look like an outage.Assuming one record. resolve4 can return several addresses. Clients are expected to try more than one.Debugging with the wrong tool. dig asks DNS directly. Your app may be using /etc/hosts. When they disagree, you are looking at two different doors.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Short TTLs let you move traffic fast (failover, migrations) but multiply resolver load and add a lookup to more requests. Long TTLs are fast and cheap but make mistakes slow to undo. Lower the TTL before a planned migration, not during it.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Every outbound call from your service starts with a lookup. At high request rates, uncached dns.lookup calls are a classic cause of mysterious latency spikes and thread-pool starvation. Cache resolved addresses in-process (respecting TTL) or put a local caching resolver next to the service. Kubernetes and service meshes lean heavily on DNS for service discovery. Short TTLs there are deliberate, and so is the need to cache sensibly on the client side.

title: TCP and the cost of a connection

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: IP delivers packets on a best-effort basis. They can be dropped, duplicated, delayed or reordered, and the network will not tell you. Almost every application wants something stronger: bytes arrive, once, in order, or I find out. TCP builds that guarantee on top of IP using sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmission. TCP moves the hard problem (loss, reordering, congestion) out of every application and into one well-tested layer in the operating system kernel.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The three-way handshake Before either side sends data, both must agree on starting sequence numbers and confirm the other is reachable. The client's first data can ride with, or right after, the final ACK. The key consequence: one full round trip passes before the first byte of your request can be acted on. With a 80 ms round trip to a server, every brand new connection costs about 80 ms before HTTP even starts. A byte stream, not messages Once established, each side sees a continuous stream. The kernel splits it into segments however it likes. This tiny server makes the point: If a client writes hello and then world quickly, the server may log one chunk of 10 bytes, or two of 5, or 3 then 7. Protocols solve this with framing: a length prefix, a delimiter such as a newline, or a header that states the body length (which is exactly what HTTP does). Loss and ordering Each segment carries a sequence number. The receiver acknowledges what it has received in order. If an acknowledgement does not arrive in time, or the sender sees duplicate ACKs, it retransmits. A lost segment therefore stalls everything behind it until it is recovered, a problem called head-of-line blocking.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Parsing a protocol by assuming one data event equals one message. It works on localhost and on your laptop, then fails under load or across a real network. Opening a new connection per request to the same host, paying the handshake every time.Ignoring errors and resets. Connections end with ECONNRESET, timeouts and half-closes. Handle error and close.Forgetting timeouts. A peer that vanishes without a FIN can leave your socket hanging for minutes by default.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Reliability and ordering cost latency: the handshake, retransmission waits and head-of-line blocking. UDP skips all of it and gives you raw datagrams, which is why real-time media, DNS queries and QUIC build their own rules on top of it.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Reuse connections. HTTP keep-alive, database connection pools and gRPC channels all exist to pay the handshake once and amortise it across many requests. Watch for ephemeral-port exhaustion and for pools sized larger than the server can accept. A server also has a listen backlog: connections that finished the handshake but have not yet been accepted by your code. If your process is too slow at calling accept, that queue fills and new clients see timeouts, even though CPU looks idle.

title: TLS: confidentiality, integrity, identity

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: A TCP connection crosses networks you do not control. Anyone on the path can read it, change it, or pretend to be the other end. TLS (Transport Layer Security) is a layer between TCP and your application protocol that fixes three problems at once: Confidentiality: observers cannot read the data.Integrity: tampering is detected.Authenticity: the client can verify it is really talking to the owner of the hostname. Encryption alone is not enough. If you encrypt to an impostor, you have just kept a secret from everyone except the attacker. Identity verification is the half people forget.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The TLS 1.3 handshake in one round trip Both sides must agree on a fresh secret key while an attacker watches every byte. They use a key exchange (ephemeral Diffie-Hellman): each side contributes a public value, and both compute the same shared secret that no eavesdropper can derive from the public values alone. After the key shares cross, everything else, including the certificate, is encrypted. TLS 1.3 needs one round trip on top of TCP's own handshake. Resumption can send application data in that first flight, at some security cost. Why the client believes the certificate A certificate says: "this public key belongs to example.com", signed by an issuer. Your operating system or browser ships a list of root certificate authorities it trusts. The server sends its certificate plus the intermediate certificates linking it to a root. The client checks: each signature in the chain verifies up to a trusted root,the certificate is within its validity dates and not revoked,the hostname the user asked for appears in the certificate,the server proves it holds the matching private key (it signs the handshake transcript). Skip any one and the guarantee collapses. Using it in Node By default Node verifies the chain and hostname and fails the connection if either is wrong. That default is the whole point.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Setting rejectUnauthorized: false (or NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0) to make a certificate error go away. This keeps encryption but removes identity checking, so anyone can intercept the connection undetected. Letting certificates expire. It is one of the most common causes of sudden outages. Automate renewal and alert well before expiry.Serving an incomplete chain. Some clients can fetch missing intermediates, others cannot, so it "works in my browser" and fails in your backend.Assuming TLS hides everything. Observers still see IPs, timing, sizes and usually the hostname via SNI.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: TLS adds a handshake round trip, CPU for key exchange and symmetric encryption, and operational work (issuance, renewal, rotation). Modern hardware makes bulk encryption cheap. The costs that remain are latency on new connections and the discipline of managing certificates.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Most teams terminate TLS at a load balancer or reverse proxy and speak plain HTTP inside a private network. That is simple, but it means internal traffic is only as safe as that network. Services handling sensitive data often use mutual TLS (both sides present certificates) inside the cluster. Track certificate expiry as a metric, not a calendar reminder. Prefer short-lived automatically renewed certificates (for example from an ACME-based CA) over certificates that live for a year and are forgotten.

title: Processes, threads and waiting for I/O

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: A request to your backend usually does very little computing. It waits for the database, waits for another service, waits for a disk. If your program stops completely during each wait, one slow query freezes everyone behind it. Scaling a server is largely the art of not wasting time while waiting. The question this lesson answers: what does your program do during the 20 ms it waits for the database?

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Process and thread A process is a running program with its own memory. A thread is a path of execution inside a process; threads of one process share its memory. Sharing is cheap and dangerous: two threads changing the same variable can corrupt it (chapter C5). Separate processes are isolated, which is safer but communication costs more. The operating system schedules threads onto CPU cores, switching between them. A switch (a context switch) saves one thread's registers and loads another's. It costs microseconds, plus cache misses afterwards. Cheap once, expensive at thousands per second. Model 1: block the thread The simplest design: one thread per request. The code reads like a script, and when it calls the database the thread blocks: the OS parks it until the answer arrives. It is easy to reason about. The cost: each thread reserves stack memory (often around a megabyte of address space) and adds scheduling work. Ten thousand waiting connections means ten thousand parked threads. Model 2: do not block, get notified Mark the socket non-blocking and ask the OS to tell you when any of many sockets is ready (epoll on Linux). One thread loops: take a ready event, run a small piece of code, go back. While the database works, that thread serves other requests. This loop is exactly what you will see step by step in the Node.js event loop lab. Node runs your JavaScript on one thread, and the loop hands it work as the OS reports readiness. "both started" prints before either file arrives because the thread moved on. The cost of this model is that your code must never block the one thread, and the code style (callbacks, promises, await) is less linear. What the single thread must never do A long loop of pure computing also blocks the loop: while it runs, no other request is served. The model works for waiting-heavy work and fails for CPU-heavy work, which you move to worker threads or other processes.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Calling a synchronous API such as fs.readFileSync or a heavy JSON.parse of a huge body inside a request handler. It looks harmless in testing and freezes every other connection under load. Confusing concurrency with parallelism, then expecting one Node process to use eight cores.Unbounded thread counts in blocking designs, which exhaust memory under a traffic spike.Starting work and forgetting to await it, so errors vanish and ordering breaks.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Thread-per-request is simple to write and debug but spends memory per waiting connection. Event-driven handles huge numbers of idle connections cheaply but demands that nothing blocks. Modern runtimes blur the line with lightweight threads, but the underlying trade remains.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Node services typically run one process per CPU core behind a load balancer or a process manager, because one process uses one core for JavaScript. CPU-heavy tasks go to worker threads or a separate service so the loop stays responsive. Teams monitor event-loop lag as a health signal.

title: The Node.js event loop, step by step

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Because your code runs on one thread, the order in which callbacks run is the order of your program's behaviour. Bugs like "why did this log appear before that one" and "why does my handler see stale data" are order bugs. A small, fixed set of rules decides the order. Learn them and you can predict it. Without the rules, async code looks random. With them, it is deterministic enough to compute by hand.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The rules, in the order they apply Run the main script to the end (the call stack empties).Run all process.nextTick callbacks, then all microtasks (promise .then and await continuations). Repeat until both queues are empty.Enter the loop. Each turn visits phases in order: timers (due setTimeout/setInterval), then poll (I/O callbacks, waiting here if nothing else is pending), then check (setImmediate).After each individual callback, step 2 happens again: nextTick and microtasks drain. A first prediction Synchronous lines first (1, 2). Then nextTick (3), then the promise microtask (4). Then the loop begins. The timer and the immediate are the interesting pair, and the next section explains why they are not guaranteed in a fixed order from the main script. Timer versus immediate setTimeout(fn, 0) really means "at least about 1 ms from now". If the main script finishes in under a millisecond, the loop may reach the timers phase before the timer is due, run poll and check first, and fire the immediate before the timeout. If the script took longer, the timeout fires first. Inside an I/O callback, however, setImmediate always fires before any timer, because the loop is already past timers heading to check. Try the lab below. It replays six programs step by step: the queues, nested scheduling, async functions, timers, I/O and the race above. The race program is flagged as non-deterministic on purpose. Starvation Because microtasks drain completely, a microtask that keeps scheduling another microtask never lets the loop move on. Timers and I/O starve. The same is true of a recursive process.nextTick. This is a real way to hang a server with no heavy computing.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Assuming setTimeout(..., 0) and setImmediate run in a guaranteed order from the main module. They do not. Only inside an I/O callback is the order fixed. Tests that rely on the race are flaky. Using nextTick to "defer a little" in library code, which can starve I/O.Forgetting that await continues as a microtask, so code after it runs before any timer.Reasoning from a browser. Browsers have a different loop model; Node's phases are specific to Node.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: The strict ordering makes code predictable but gives you tools that can starve the loop (nextTick, microtask chains). Prefer promises for ordinary async, and setImmediate or a timer when you truly want to let other work run first.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Services export an event-loop lag metric: how late a scheduled timer fires compared with when it was due. Rising lag means something is hogging the thread: a CPU-heavy handler, a synchronous call, or a microtask loop. It is one of the best single health signals for a Node service.

title: Processes, signals and exit codes

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Before frameworks and containers there is a process: a running program with its own memory, environment variables and open files. Every deploy tool, process manager and container runtime does the same few things to it: start it, send it signals, and read how it exited. Debugging "why did my service restart" starts here. A container is mostly a process with some isolation around it. If you understand signals and exit codes, you understand most of what an orchestrator is telling you.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Processes and their environment A process has a numeric id (PID), a parent, an environment (key-value strings inherited from its parent) and numbered file descriptors: 0 is standard input, 1 standard output, 2 standard error, and every open file or socket gets the next number. A child inherits a copy of its parent's exported variables, and changes it makes never flow back: This is why configuration works through the environment (B11) and why a variable set in one terminal is invisible in another. Signals A signal is a small notification the kernel delivers to a process. The ones that matter: SIGTERM (15): "please stop". The default for kill, for docker stop and for orchestrators. A program can catch it and shut down cleanly (next chapters).SIGINT (2): Ctrl+C.SIGKILL (9): stop now. It cannot be caught, blocked or ignored; no cleanup code runs.SIGHUP (1): terminal closed; often reused to mean "reload config". Test on a server that takes 1.5 seconds to answer, sending SIGTERM 0.4 seconds into a request: The default action for SIGTERM is to terminate immediately. Handling it is what makes a deploy invisible to users, the subject of the graceful shutdown chapter. Exit codes When a process ends it returns a small integer. 0 means success; anything else means failure. If a signal killed it, shells report 128 plus the signal number: a process ended by SIGTERM shows 143 (128 + 15), and one ended by SIGKILL shows 137 (128 + 9). A container that "exited with 137" was killed without cleanup, very often because it exceeded its memory limit or its stop timeout. Pipes a | b connects a's standard output to b's standard input; both run at once and data streams between them. The exit status trap: A CI script like build | tee log.txt can report success while build failed. Start scripts with set -euo pipefail (stop on error, error on unset variables, honour pipeline failures).

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Starting your server with a wrapper shell script (sh -c "node server.js") so that SIGTERM goes to the shell and never reaches Node. Use exec node server.js so the server replaces the shell as the process receiving signals. Using kill -9 as the first resort, skipping cleanup and corrupting state.Ignoring exit codes in scripts and CI.Assuming a variable set in one process reaches another without export or a restart.Leaking file descriptors, which eventually hits the per-process limit and fails with "too many open files".Reading logs only from stdout when errors go to stderr.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Graceful stop (SIGTERM, then wait, then SIGKILL after a timeout) protects in-flight work but delays deploys if the program is slow to exit. Immediate kill is fast and risks lost work. Set the grace period from how long a request or job really takes.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Know what stops your service (orchestrator, deploy, autoscaler, out-of-memory killer), log the signal and exit code on shutdown, make the main process PID 1 or use a tiny init that forwards signals, and alert on restarts with code 137.

title: Files, permissions and a reproducible dev environment

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Many backend problems are not logic bugs: "permission denied", "address already in use", "too many open files", "works on my laptop". The tools to answer them are few and old, and a short tour makes you effective on any server. When something fails outside your code, you need to look at the process from the outside. These commands turn guesses into observations.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Permissions Each file has an owner, a group and three sets of bits (owner, group, others) for read (r), write (w) and execute (x). ls -l shows them as -rw-r--r--: the owner can read and write, everyone else can read. chmod 600 file makes it -rw-------, readable only by its owner, the right mode for a private key. A new file's mode comes from the creator's umask: with umask 022 a new file was -rw-r--r--, and with umask 077 it was -rw-------. Directories need execute permission to be entered. A service should run as its own unprivileged user with access only to what it needs (its data directory, its config), never as root. Containers inherit the same rule: add a USER instruction in the Dockerfile. Looking at a running system ps aux or pgrep -a node: which processes exist and with what command line.ss -ltnp: which process is listening on which port. This answers "address already in use" (a stale process holds the port).lsof -p PID: files and sockets a process has open; shows file-descriptor leaks and what it is connected to.curl -v and curl -w for HTTP; jq to read JSON responses.strace -p PID: the system calls a process makes; the last call before a hang often explains it ("stuck in read on socket 9, waiting for the database"). It slows the process, so use it briefly.ulimit -n: the maximum open file descriptors per process. A busy server that accepts many connections needs this raised from a small default; hitting it produces "too many open files". Pipes and text tools grep, sort, uniq -c, wc, awk and jq chained with pipes answer most log questions in one line, for example counting error types or the slowest endpoints. Remember set -o pipefail in scripts. A reproducible environment "Works on my machine" is usually unpinned versions. Make setup boring: Pin the runtime version (.nvmrc or engines in package.json, .python-version).Commit the lockfile (pnpm-lock.yaml, poetry.lock) and install from it with the frozen flag in CI.Keep a .env.example listing every variable (B11) and a short README with exact commands.Provide one command to start dependencies (a Docker Compose file or a script) and one to run tests.Run the same checks in CI that you run locally. The test: can a new teammate go from clone to running tests in minutes by following the README without asking you anything?

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: chmod 777 to make an error go away. It lets every user on the machine modify the file. Find out which user needs which access and grant exactly that. Running as root inside containers and on servers.Committing .env files or private keys, or leaving them world-readable.Killing the process holding a port without checking what it is.Different runtime versions between laptop, CI and production.Undocumented manual setup steps that exist only in someone's head.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Strict permissions and unprivileged users cost occasional setup friction and prevent large incidents. A fully containerised dev environment is reproducible but slower to iterate on than running tools natively; many teams run dependencies in containers and the app natively.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Run services under dedicated users with minimal rights, set explicit file-descriptor limits, keep read-only filesystems where possible, record the exact runtime and dependency versions of every deploy, and practise diagnosing a hung process with ss, lsof and strace before you need to.

title: HTTP as text on a socket

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Clients and servers written by different people, in different languages, years apart, need to agree on how to ask for something and how to answer. HTTP is that agreement: a small set of rules for a request and a response, simple enough to implement in an afternoon and general enough to carry web pages, JSON APIs and file downloads. Keeping the protocol text-based and stateless made it easy to debug, cache and scale. Any server can answer any request, so you can put many servers behind one address.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The shape of a message Here is a complete request, exactly as it travels over the wire. Lines end with \r\n, and a blank line ends the headers. The request line: method, target, version.Headers: Name: value metadata. Host is required in HTTP/1.1 because one IP can serve many sites.An empty line.An optional body, whose length is declared by a header. The response mirrors it: The status line replaces the request line. Then headers, a blank line, and the body. How does the reader know where the body ends? TCP is a byte stream, so HTTP must say. Either Content-Length: N gives the exact byte count, or Transfer-Encoding: chunked sends the body in length-prefixed pieces, ending with a zero-length chunk. No framework can guess this; it is part of the protocol. Speaking HTTP with a raw socket Run it and curl -i localhost:8080/hello. The same server in Node's http module is five lines, but it does exactly this parsing for you, plus all the edge cases this toy ignores (partial buffers, request bodies, pipelining, malformed input). Statelessness The server keeps nothing about you between requests. If request two depends on request one, the client must say so: a cookie, an Authorization header, an id in the URL. This is why any replica can serve any request.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Wrong Content-Length. Too small and the client truncates your response. Too large and it hangs waiting for bytes that never come. Count bytes, not characters: "é" is one character and two bytes in UTF-8. Forgetting the blank line between headers and body.Trusting the client's headers. Host, X-Forwarded-For and Content-Length are claims, not facts.Putting secrets in the URL. URLs end up in logs, history and referrer headers.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Text headers are easy to read and extend but verbose and repeated on every request. HTTP/2 compresses headers and multiplexes many requests over one connection, which removes HTTP-level head-of-line blocking but not TCP's. HTTP/3 moves to QUIC to remove that too. The semantics you learn here stay the same across all three.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: You almost never see raw bytes in production, but you will meet their consequences: proxies that enforce header size limits, load balancers that close idle keep-alive connections, and request-smuggling bugs where two parsers disagree about where a message ends. When a client and a proxy disagree about the body length, an attacker can hide a second request inside the first. This is why strict, boring parsing matters.

title: Methods, status codes and the headers that matter

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: A request must say what you want done, and a response must say how it went, in a way that software you did not write (browsers, CDNs, proxies, retry libraries) can act on without understanding your business. Methods and status codes are that shared vocabulary. The precise meaning of GET, PUT and 404 is what lets a CDN cache your pages and a client safely retry a failed request. Meanings are contracts, not decoration.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Methods and their guarantees Safe means the request does not change server state, so it can be prefetched and cached freely.Idempotent means doing it once or ten times leaves the same final state, so a client may retry after a timeout. MethodSafeIdempotentTypical useGETyesyesread a resourceHEADyesyesheaders onlyPUTnoyesreplace a resourceDELETEnoyesremove a resourcePOSTnonocreate or run an actionPATCHnonot guaranteedpartial update Idempotent describes the effect on state, not the response: a second DELETE may return 404, but the end state is identical. Status families RangeMeaningExamples2xxsuccess200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content3xxgo elsewhere or use your copy301 Moved, 304 Not Modified4xxthe client's request is wrong400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 4295xxthe server failed500, 502, 503, 504 Notice 401 means "I do not know who you are" and 403 means "I know who you are and the answer is no". The headers you will use daily Content-Type states how to interpret the body (application/json).Accept states what the client can handle.Authorization carries credentials.Cache-Control states how long and by whom a response may be reused.ETag is a version fingerprint for a response. Conditional requests: saving the body The client says "I already have version v17". If it is still current, the server answers 304 with no body, and the client reuses its copy. One round trip, almost no bytes.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Using GET for actions with side effects, such as GET /delete?id=5. Browsers prefetch links, crawlers follow them, and caches may replay them. A harmless-looking page load can delete data. Everything is 200 or 500. Return the most specific code you can; clients branch on it.Retrying non-idempotent requests blindly. A retried POST /charge can charge twice.Confusing 401 and 403, which breaks client login flows.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Strict semantics make your API predictable and cacheable, but real operations do not always fit. A "cancel order" action is awkward as a pure resource update. Prefer honouring the guarantees (safe, idempotent) over matching a verb to a sentence.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Retries are where semantics pay off. Because PUT and DELETE are idempotent, retry middleware can repeat them. For POST, make your own operations idempotent with an idempotency key so a retry after a timeout does not duplicate the effect. Status codes also drive your dashboards: error rate is usually the share of 5xx, and a spike in 429 tells you clients are being rate limited.

title: CORS: why browsers police cross-origin calls

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Your browser holds your cookies for your bank. Imagine you also open evil.example in another tab. Its JavaScript could call bank.example/transfer, and the browser would attach your bank cookies automatically. Worse, it could read the answers. The same-origin policy prevents the reading part: a page may only read responses from its own origin, the triple of scheme, host and port. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is how a server says "this other origin is allowed to read my responses." The browser cannot know which cross-origin reads are legitimate. Only the server can say so, and CORS is the protocol for saying it.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: What counts as the same origin https://app.example.com compared with: https://app.example.com/other is same-origin (path does not matter).http://app.example.com is different (scheme).https://api.example.com is different (host).https://app.example.com:8443 is different (port). Simple requests For basic requests (GET, HEAD, or POST with a form-like content type, no unusual headers) the browser sends the request with an Origin header and then looks at the answer: If the allow header matches the page's origin, JavaScript may read the response. If not, the browser discards it and logs a CORS error. The request was still sent. Preflighted requests If the request could have side effects the server never expected from a browser, such as a PUT, a custom header like Authorization, or Content-Type: application/json, the browser first asks permission with an OPTIONS request: Only if the preflight answer permits the method and headers does the real request go out. A correct handler The credentials rule matters: when a request includes cookies, the server cannot answer Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *. It must name the exact origin.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Reflecting whatever Origin arrives (Allow-Origin: <anything>) together with Allow-Credentials: true. That authorises every website on earth to read your users' private data. Always check the origin against an allowlist. Forgetting Vary: Origin, so a shared cache serves one origin's allow header to another origin.Not handling OPTIONS. Your router returns 404 or 405 to the preflight and the real call never happens.Treating CORS as access control. Anyone can call your API directly. Authenticate and authorise on the server.Disabling it everywhere in dev and shipping that. Use an explicit allowlist per environment.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: The easiest fix for CORS pain is to avoid it: serve the frontend and API from the same origin, or put them behind one reverse proxy. You lose independent deployment hostnames but gain simplicity, no preflights and safer cookies. A public, read-only API can safely use a wildcard origin without credentials.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Preflights add a round trip to many calls. Set a sensible Access-Control-Max-Age so browsers cache the permission, and watch for gateways or CDNs that strip or overwrite your CORS headers. Check the whole path, not only your app. When debugging, open the browser's Network tab and look at the actual OPTIONS response headers. The console message tells you what failed; the headers tell you why.

title: Routes are a lookup table

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: After the HTTP request is parsed you have a method such as GET and a path such as /users/42/posts. Something must decide which of your functions should run. Hard-coding a giant if over strings does not scale, so every framework keeps a route table: a list of (method, pattern, handler) entries. Routing separates "what URL was asked for" from "what code answers it", so you can add an endpoint without touching the others.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Patterns and parameters A pattern is a path with holes. /users/:id has a hole called id. To match, split into segments: literal segments must be equal, :name segments accept any non-empty text without a slash, and the captured text becomes a parameter. That is a working router in about twenty lines. The query string is cut off first because it is not part of the path. Parameters are percent-decoded, so /users/a%2Fb gives the id a/b. 404 versus 405 If no pattern fits the path, the answer is 404 Not Found. If the path fits at least one pattern but with another method, the answer is 405 Method Not Allowed, with an Allow header naming the methods that do work. The router above collects those methods while it scans. Cost Scanning the list is O(R) regexp tests for R routes. For a few hundred routes that is microseconds and irrelevant next to a database call. Large frameworks compile all routes into a trie (a tree keyed by path segment) so lookup depends on the URL's length, not the number of routes.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Returning 404 for a valid path with the wrong method. Clients and developers lose the hint that the URL is right and only the verb is wrong. Return 405 with an Allow header. Forgetting that parameters are strings. The id is "42", not 42. Convert and validate it.Trusting decoded parameters. decodeURIComponent can produce /, .. and other surprises. Never join a parameter into a file path without validating it.Throwing on bad encoding. decodeURIComponent("%E0%A4%A") throws. A hostile URL must produce a 400, not a crash.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: A route table is simple, explicit and easy to read, but in a list the first match wins, so order matters (next lesson). Declarative routing (file-system routes, decorators) hides the table but does not remove the rules.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Frameworks report the matched pattern (such as /users/:id) rather than the raw URL to logs and metrics. Raw URLs contain ids and create millions of distinct metric labels; the pattern keeps the cardinality small and the dashboards usable.

title: Order, specificity and edge cases

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Real route tables overlap. /users/me is a specific page; /users/:id is the general case. Both match /users/me. Something must break the tie, and if you do not know the rule, you get bugs where the wrong handler runs and everything looks fine in tests that use the other URL. Overlaps are normal. The tie-break rule is part of your API's behaviour, so you should know it and test it.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: First match wins A router walks its list in registration order and stops at the first route that fits. So specific routes go first: Swap those two lines and a request for /users/me is answered by the general route with id equal to "me". I ran this in Express 5 to check: the swapped order returns param:me. This is called shadowing. Edge cases and what Express does by default RequestExpress 5 defaultWhy it mattersGET /users/42/ (trailing slash)Matches /users/:idTwo URLs serve one resource unless you redirectGET /Users/42 (different case)MatchesSame: duplicates for caches and search enginesPOST /users/42 (no such route)404A 405 with an Allow header would be more helpfulGET /users/a%2Fbid is a/bDecoded value can contain a slash All four were checked against a running Express 5 server. Frameworks differ, so check yours instead of assuming. Choose a policy, then enforce it A canonical URL is the one agreed spelling. Pick one (for example lower case, no trailing slash), and redirect the others with a 301 or reject them. Otherwise caches store several copies, analytics split, and an authorisation rule written for one spelling might not apply to another. Where it bites security Authorisation often hangs off a path prefix, such as "everything under /admin needs an admin". If the router treats /admin and /ADMIN/ as the same route but the guard compares exact strings, one spelling slips past. Put access checks on the router or the handler, not on string comparisons of the raw URL.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Registering the general route first. Everything works for ids, and the one special word, such as me, never reaches its handler. Put specific routes before parameterised ones, and add a test for each special word. Prefix checks on raw paths for authorisation, which differ on case, slashes and encoding.A catch-all (*) registered early, which hides every route after it.No fallback, so unknown paths return a framework HTML page instead of your JSON error.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Being lenient (accepting trailing slashes and any case) is friendly to humans, but creates duplicate URLs and subtle security gaps. Being strict is safer and cacheable, but breaks sloppy clients. Many APIs choose strict plus a redirect from the common mistakes.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Teams keep a test that lists every route with a few awkward URLs (trailing slash, upper case, encoded slash, wrong method) and asserts the exact status code. It documents the policy and catches a framework upgrade that changes a default. A final JSON 404 handler and an error handler close the table, so every unknown path gets a consistent, machine-readable answer.

title: Text, bytes and JSON

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Your program holds objects. A socket carries only bytes. Serialization is the conversion from objects to bytes, and deserialization is the way back. Every request body and response body goes through it. If the two ends disagree about how, data is corrupted without any error. Every integration bug of the form "it worked on my machine, but the other service saw different data" is a serialization disagreement.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Characters versus bytes UTF-8 encodes each character in 1 to 4 bytes: plain ASCII takes 1, many accented letters take 2, most Asian scripts 3, emoji 4. I ran this to check: Three different answers for one string. The wire cares about the middle one: Content-Length and any size limit are in bytes. If you compute it with s.length you will truncate or hang a response that contains non-ASCII text. Encoding must be agreed The same character is different bytes in different encodings: é is c3 a9 in UTF-8 but e9 in Latin-1. Declare it (Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8; JSON is UTF-8 by standard) and decode with the declared one. What JSON can and cannot say JSON has objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. That is all. Checking in Node: Dates have no JSON type; they become strings. Use ISO 8601 UTC (2026-11-22T08:00:00Z) and parse them explicitly.Numbers are floats in JavaScript. Integers above 2^53 (9,007,199,254,740,992) lose precision. Send big ids and money as strings (or integers in the smallest unit, such as paise).undefined and functions vanish; NaN and Infinity become null. Money and floats 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in JSON too. Never use floats for money: store integer minor units and format on display.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Sending a 64-bit database id as a JSON number. A JavaScript client reads it as a float and the last digits change, so it requests a different record. Send such ids as strings. Computing sizes with string.length for headers or limits.Trusting parse success as validity. Valid JSON can still be the wrong shape; validate it (chapter A5).Letting JSON.parse exceptions become 500s. Malformed client input is a 400.Putting dates in local time without an offset.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: JSON is human readable, universal and easy to debug, but verbose, weakly typed and slower to parse than binary formats. For public APIs and most services, that trade is right. The next lesson covers when a binary format is worth its cost.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Set a maximum request body size (this API uses 256 KB for JSON) so a client cannot send a gigabyte to parse, and log parse failures at a low level. Use ISO 8601 UTC for every timestamp and document how big numbers are sent.

title: Binary formats, schemas and compatibility

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: JSON repeats every field name in every message and writes numbers as text. For a service that sends millions of small messages to another service, that is wasted bandwidth and CPU. A schema-based binary format agrees the field layout in advance, so the message carries only values and short numeric tags. When both sides share a schema, names do not need to travel. That is where the size and speed come from, and also where the new problems come from.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Varints: small numbers take fewer bytes A varint stores an unsigned integer 7 bits at a time. Each byte holds 7 bits of the number; the top bit says "more bytes follow". Small numbers fit in one byte. I ran this: 1 encodes as 01 and 300 as ac 02. The cost is one byte per 7 bits of the value, so the size depends on how large the number is, not on the field type. A whole message by hand Take the schema message User { int32 id = 1; string name = 2; } and the value { id: 150, name: "ada" }. Each field is written as a tag (the field number shifted left 3 bits, OR the wire type) followed by its value. BytesMeaning08tag: field 1, wire type 0 (varint)96 01varint 15012tag: field 2, wire type 2 (length-delimited)03length 361 64 61the UTF-8 bytes of "ada" Total: 08 96 01 12 03 61 64 61 is 8 bytes. The equivalent JSON text {"id":150,"name":"ada"} is 23 bytes. (Both counts were produced by running the code.) Why field numbers are forever The reader uses the tag to know which field it is looking at. That makes evolution possible if you follow the rules: Safe: add a new field with a new number (old readers skip unknown tags); stop using a field and mark its number reserved; rename a field (names are not on the wire).Breaking: reuse a number for a different meaning; change a field's type to an incompatible one. The cost you accept You cannot read the bytes with your eyes, you need the schema and code generation, and tooling like curl and browser dev tools understand JSON better than Protobuf. That is the real price of the savings.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Reusing a retired field number for a new field. An old client that still sends the old meaning will write data the new server interprets as the new meaning, and nothing fails loudly. Making every field required. You can never remove one later. Treat fields as optional by default.Switching formats for speed without measuring. Network and database time usually dominate parsing time.Using floats for money in a schema as well, with the same errors as JSON.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Binary formats reduce size and parse time and give strong contracts, at the price of tooling, readability and a build step. They shine for internal service-to-service calls at high volume. Public, browser-facing APIs usually stay on JSON.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Schema files live in version control with a compatibility check in CI (tools such as buf compare the new schema to the previous release and fail on breaking changes). Retired field numbers are marked reserved so nobody reuses them. gRPC, covered in a later chapter, is built on exactly this.

title: Passwords and server-side sessions

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: HTTP forgets everything between requests. Yet an app must know that this request comes from the same person who logged in a minute ago, and it must not trust a client that simply claims "I am user 7". Two separate problems follow: Authentication: proving who the caller is.Authorization: deciding what that caller may do. This lesson covers authentication. The next covers tokens and authorization. Authentication is the first thing an attacker targets and the thing users reuse across sites, so mistakes here leak accounts everywhere.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Storing passwords Never store the password. Store the output of a password hash: a one-way function made deliberately slow and memory-hungry (scrypt, argon2, bcrypt). Add a random salt per user so equal passwords produce different hashes and precomputed tables are useless. Slowness is the point: a legitimate login hashes once, which costs tens of milliseconds, while an attacker with a stolen table must try billions of guesses. timingSafeEqual avoids leaking how many leading bytes matched through response time. Real systems usually use a vetted library for argon2 or bcrypt so parameters and encoding are handled for you. The example shows the idea with what ships in Node. Sessions After the password check succeeds, the server creates a session: a record such as { id, userId, expiresAt } in a store, keyed by a long random id. It sends the id to the browser in a cookie. Every later request carries the cookie, the server looks the id up, and finds the user. The id must be unguessable: 128 bits or more from a cryptographic random source. Because the server holds the state, it can revoke instantly: delete the record and the cookie stops working. Cookie flags HttpOnly: scripts cannot read it, limiting the damage of cross-site scripting.Secure: sent only over HTTPS.SameSite: restricts sending on cross-site requests, a main defence against cross-site request forgery. See the CORS lesson for how it differs from cross-origin rules.Max-Age / Expires: bounds the session lifetime.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Putting the user id itself in the cookie (uid=7). A client can change it to 8. The cookie must be an opaque random id that only means something inside your server's store. Fast hashes such as plain SHA-256 for passwords, which attackers compute at billions per second.Telling the user which half was wrong. "No such email" versus "wrong password" lets attackers enumerate accounts. Return one generic message.No login rate limiting, which permits unlimited guessing.Not rotating the session id after login, which enables session fixation.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Server-side sessions are easy to revoke and keep secrets off the client, but every request needs a lookup and the store becomes shared infrastructure that must be fast and available across all server copies. Putting sessions in a fast store such as Redis is the common answer.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Run the session store outside the app processes so every copy sees the same sessions, set a sensible idle and absolute expiry, delete sessions on logout and on password change, and log sign-ins and failures. Prefer a maintained auth library or a hosted identity service to hand-rolled code.

title: JWTs, trade-offs and authorization

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Sessions need a lookup in a shared store on every request. A JSON Web Token carries the identity inside itself, signed by the server, so any server copy can verify it with a key and no store. That is attractive for many servers, or for several services that should all accept the same login. The token moves the state from the server to the client and replaces a lookup with a signature check.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The three parts A JWT is three base64url pieces joined by dots: header (algorithm), payload (claims such as user id and expiry), and signature. The signature is computed over the first two with a secret (or a private key). On each request the server recomputes it. If the payload were altered, the signature would not match. This is a teaching sketch. In real code, use a maintained JWT library, pin the accepted algorithm yourself, and never accept the algorithm named in an incoming token header blindly. Accepting "none" or a swapped algorithm has caused real breaches. What it does not do The payload is readable by anyone. Do not put secrets in it. And because no server record exists, you cannot simply delete a token: it stays valid until it expires. The usual compromise is a short-lived access token (minutes) plus a refresh token stored server-side that can be revoked and exchanged for new access tokens. Sessions versus JWTs JWTs shine when verification must happen in many places without a shared database. For one ordinary web app, a server-side session is simpler and easier to revoke. Choose with a reason, not a trend. Authorization Once you know who is calling, check what they may do: Role-based: admins may delete users, members may not.Ownership: a user may read their own invoice. Skipping the ownership line is the classic IDOR (insecure direct object reference): any logged-in user changes the number in the URL and reads someone else's data. Returning 404 for both missing and forbidden avoids revealing which ids exist.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Checking only that a user is logged in, not that they own the object. This is among the most common serious API bugs, because the code works perfectly in testing with one user. Long-lived JWTs with no revocation path.Storing a token where scripts can read it (such as localStorage) without weighing the cross-site scripting risk, versus an HttpOnly cookie.Trusting claims such as role: admin that the client could have forged, when the signature is not actually verified.Doing authorization only in the UI, by hiding buttons.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Sessions: easy revocation, a lookup per request, shared store required. JWTs: no lookup and easy to verify anywhere, but hard to revoke and larger on every request. Many systems use both: a short JWT at the edge, a revocable refresh session behind it.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Keep signing keys in a secrets manager and support key rotation. Keep access tokens short, log authorization failures, and write tests that log in as user A and try to read and change user B's objects. That one test finds more real bugs than most reviews.

title: Never trust input: validate at the edge

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Your server's job begins where someone else's program ends. A request body, a query string, a header, a cookie, a path segment and an uploaded file are all text chosen by whoever sent them. That line between "bytes I received" and "values my code can rely on" is the trust boundary. Code deep inside your program makes assumptions: age is a number, email is a string, items is an array. If those assumptions are false you get crashes at best and security holes at worst. Validation is how you turn "whatever arrived" into "something my code is allowed to assume". Check once, at the boundary, and produce a trusted value. Then the rest of the program can be written without defensive checks on every line.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Reject, do not repair Prefer an allow-list: describe exactly what is valid and refuse everything else. A deny-list ("reject strings containing <script>") always misses a variant you did not think of. A parser takes untrusted input and returns either a clean value or a set of field errors: Three things to notice. It checks the type first (a number sent as the string "30" is rejected, not guessed at). It collects all errors so the caller fixes everything in one round trip. And on success it builds a new object from named fields. Mass assignment That last point matters. Suppose the handler did db.users.insert(req.body). A client who adds "isAdmin": true to the JSON has just promoted themselves. Building the value from explicit fields means anything you did not name is dropped: Three different jobs JobQuestion it answersExampleValidateIs this acceptable at all?reject age: "abc" with 400NormaliseIs there one canonical form?trim and lower-case an emailEscapeIs it safe in this output?HTML-encode when rendering, parameterise SQL Validation does not make a value safe for every sink. A perfectly valid name such as O'Brien still breaks naive string-built SQL. Escape or parameterise at the point of use, and validate at the point of entry.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Trusting the browser form. The frontend check improves the experience; the server check is the only one that protects you. Validating only some fields and passing the rest of the object through.Checking after use, for example reading req.body.limit into a database query before validating it.Silent repair. Turning "abc" into 0 hides bugs in clients and attacks alike.Checking the type loosely. age == 30 is true for the string "30".Unbounded input. Without maximum lengths and body-size limits, a valid-looking 500 MB string is a denial of service.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Strict validation rejects some clients that were "almost right", which can break integrations. Lenient validation keeps them working but spreads ambiguity into your data. Be strict about what you accept now; you can always loosen later, but you can rarely tighten a rule that clients already depend on.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Describe input once as a schema (a validation library or JSON Schema) rather than hand-writing checks per route, set a maximum request body size, and return a consistent error shape. Log rejected requests at a low level: a spike of validation failures is often the first sign of a probing attacker or a broken client release.

title: Coercion, defaults and error responses

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Validation (the previous lesson) decides what is acceptable. This lesson covers the awkward middle step: turning loosely typed input into the exact types your code wants, and telling the caller clearly when that fails. JSON preserves numbers, booleans and null. A query string preserves nothing: /items?limit=10&active=true delivers the text "10" and the text "true". Path parameters, headers and form bodies are text too. Convert once, in the same place you validate, so the rest of the code receives real numbers and booleans and never has to wonder.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: JavaScript's conversions are forgiving This prints 0 0 0 NaN and then NaN 12 16 1000. An empty string becomes 0, parseInt stops at the first bad character and returns 12 for "12abc", and hexadecimal and exponent forms are accepted. If ?limit= (empty) quietly becomes 0, your pagination silently misbehaves. Check the string with a pattern first, then convert: Defaults are applied here, in one place, instead of being scattered as limit || 20 across handlers. (|| is a classic bug source: it also replaces a legitimate 0.) Repeated and unknown keys The same key can appear twice. With the standard URL API, get returns the first value and getAll returns every value: Frameworks differ in what they hand you (a string, the last value, or an array), so a validator should say which it accepts and reject the rest. For unknown fields in a JSON body choose a policy deliberately: strip them (lenient, common for public APIs), or reject them (strict, catches typos such as emial). Either is fine; accidentally passing them through is not. Duplicate keys in JSON JSON text such as {"a":1,"a":2} parses to { a: 2 } in JavaScript: the last one wins. Other languages may keep the first. If two components disagree about which wins, an attacker can show one value to a checker and another to the code that acts on it. Parse once and pass the parsed object around, never the raw text. Error responses Return 400 Bad Request for malformed or invalid input (some teams use 422 Unprocessable Content for "well-formed but semantically invalid"; pick one and be consistent). Include enough for a client to fix the request, and nothing about your internals: A stable machine-readable code, a human message, and per-field details. RFC 9457 standardises a similar "problem details" shape if you want an existing convention.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Using parseInt or Number straight on user input and trusting the result. parseInt("12abc") is 12 and Number("") is 0: the bad input became a plausible value. Using || for defaults, which also overrides 0 and the empty string.Leaking internals in errors: stack traces, SQL fragments or file paths.Different error shapes per endpoint, which forces every client to special-case each route.Returning 200 with an error in the body, which breaks caches, monitoring and generic clients.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Strict conversion ("must be digits only") gives precise errors but rejects limit=10.0 or limit=+10. Lenient conversion accepts more but multiplies the ways one value can be written, which makes caching, logging and security rules harder. Public APIs lean strict and document the exact format.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Put coercion and defaults in the schema so they are declared, tested and documented in one place. Cap array lengths, string lengths and pagination sizes. Count validation failures per route and per client in your metrics.

title: Layers: controllers, services and repositories

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Early on, one function does everything: parse the request, check the rules, run SQL, build the response. It works for ten endpoints. At fifty, a change to the database layout touches every handler, a rule such as "no negative transfers" is copied in four places, and testing anything needs a running server and database. The fix is not a framework feature. It is deciding that each piece of code has one reason to change. Three layers give three seams: you can test rules with plain function calls, replace storage without touching rules, and change URL shapes without touching either.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: LayerKnows aboutDoes not know aboutController (route handler)requests, responses, status codes, validationSQL, business rulesService (use case)business rules, transactions, other servicesHTTP, request or response objectsRepositorystorage queries and mapping rows to objectsHTTP, business rules Here is a money transfer in all three, runnable as plain Node. The repository is an in-memory map; in a real service its two methods would run SQL. Running it gives these results. Moving 30 from account 1 to account 2 returns { status: 204 } and leaves balances 70 and 35. Asking account 2 to send 500 returns 409, an unknown account returns 404, and an amount of -3 returns 400. Notice three things: transfer takes the repository as an argument. That is dependency injection in its simplest form: a test passes a fake repository and needs no database.The service throws a domain error (InsufficientFunds), not an HTTP status. Only the controller decides that this means 409. A queue worker calling the same service would map it differently.Validation of the shape of the request (is amount a positive integer?) lives in the controller; the rule "balance must cover the amount" lives in the service. Where does a transaction go? The service decides what must succeed or fail together, so it owns the transaction boundary, and the repository executes inside it. In this toy the two save calls are not atomic: a crash between them loses money. The transactions chapter (B4) shows how to fix that properly.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Passing the framework's request object into the service. The service now cannot be called from a job or a test without faking HTTP, and the layers have merged again under another name. "Anemic" pass-through layers where the service only forwards to the repository and adds nothing.Repositories containing business rules such as "apply the discount here".Returning database rows straight to the client, which freezes your table layout into your public API.Catching every error in the controller and returning 500, which hides the domain errors you wanted to map.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Layers add files, names and indirection. For a handful of simple CRUD endpoints a single function per route is clearer. Introduce the split when rules start to repeat, when you need tests without a server, or when more than one entry point (HTTP, queue, CLI) must run the same logic.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Keep a single place that maps domain errors to HTTP responses, so every endpoint answers the same way. Pass dependencies in explicitly at start-up instead of importing singletons, which makes the wiring visible and tests easy. Log at the service layer with business meaning ("transfer rejected, insufficient funds") and at the edge with HTTP meaning.

title: Middleware: a pipeline around your handler

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Some work applies to many routes: parse the body, attach a request id, check who the caller is, measure the time taken, apply a rate limit, turn errors into responses. Copying those lines into every handler is repetitive and easy to forget on one route, and a forgotten authentication check is a vulnerability. Middleware extracts that work into small functions arranged in a chain around the handler. These are cross-cutting concerns: things that cut across features rather than belonging to one. A pipeline lets you state "every request is timed, authenticated, then handled" once, in one place, and makes a missing step impossible rather than unlikely.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Each middleware receives the request and a next function. Calling next() hands control to the following one; returning without calling it stops the chain. A minimal runner shows the whole idea: Now three middleware: one times the request, one rejects anonymous callers, one is the handler. For an anonymous request the log reads timing:in > auth > timing:out with status 401. The handler never ran: auth short-circuited by not calling next. For a signed-in request it reads timing:in > auth > handler > timing:out with status 200. Look at timing:out. It runs after the rest of the chain finished, because await next() returns only once everything downstream has completed. That "on the way out" phase is how loggers record the final status and duration. Order is behaviour A request-id middleware belongs first, so every later log line has an id.Body parsing and size limits come before anything that reads the body.Authentication comes before authorization and before the handlers it protects.A rate limiter often goes before expensive work such as parsing or password hashing.The error handler goes last, because it must catch what everything above throws. Errors If a middleware or handler throws, the rejection travels back up through the chain. One middleware near the top can catch it and translate it to a response, so no handler needs its own try/catch: Running it leaves status 500 and the message db down. In Express the equivalent is a function with four parameters (err, req, res, next) registered last; Express 5 also forwards rejected promises from async handlers to it automatically. The n <= i check in compose catches a classic bug: calling next() twice, which would run the rest of the chain twice and usually try to send two responses.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Forgetting to call next() (or to respond) on a branch. The request hangs, the client waits for its timeout, and the connection stays open on your server. Wrong order, such as authorization before authentication, or parsing the body before enforcing a size limit.Calling next() and then also sending a response, which tries to answer twice.Stashing per-request data in module-level variables. Concurrent requests overwrite each other. Attach data to the request object (or an async-local context) instead.Heavy synchronous work in a global middleware, which blocks the event loop for every request.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: A global pipeline is powerful but implicit: the behaviour of a route depends on code registered elsewhere, and a wrong order is invisible in the route file. Explicit per-route composition is easier to read but easy to forget. Many teams apply security and observability globally, and opt in to everything else per route.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Write the middleware order down in one file and test it: a request without credentials must be rejected, an oversized body must be refused, and an error must produce your standard error shape. Keep each middleware small and fast, and measure the pipeline's total overhead per request.

title: REST in practice: resources, status codes and idempotency

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: An API is a contract used by code you do not control. Without conventions every endpoint invents its own verbs (/getUser, /doPaymentNow) and every client must learn each one. HTTP already provides a vocabulary: URLs name things, methods say what to do with them, status codes say what happened. Using it consistently lets caches, proxies, client libraries and new teammates behave correctly without special knowledge. Predictability is the product of an API. When a method means what its name says, a client can retry, cache or batch it safely without reading your documentation.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Nouns in the URL, verbs in the method RequestMeaningGET /orders/42read order 42GET /orders?status=openlist orders, filteredPOST /orderscreate a new order; the server chooses its idPUT /orders/42replace order 42 entirely with the bodyPATCH /orders/42change only the fields in the bodyDELETE /orders/42remove order 42 Use plural collections and nest only to express real ownership (/orders/42/items). Avoid verbs in paths; when an action does not fit a noun (cancel an order), model it as a sub-resource or a state change (POST /orders/42/cancellation) rather than inventing /cancelOrder. Safe and idempotent A method is safe if it does not change server state: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS.A method is idempotent if doing it N times leaves the same state as doing it once: GET, PUT, DELETE (and the safe ones). POST is not, and PATCH is not guaranteed to be. This is not trivia: it decides what a client or proxy may do after a timeout, when it cannot know whether the request arrived. Status codes that tell the truth CodeUse it when200 OKsuccess with a body201 CreatedPOST made a resource; add a Location header with its URL204 No Contentsuccess, nothing to return (often DELETE, PUT)400 Bad Requestmalformed or invalid input401 / 403not authenticated / authenticated but not allowed404 Not Foundno such resource409 Conflictvalid request that clashes with current state (duplicate, version mismatch)422 Unprocessable Contentwell-formed but fails semantic rules (some teams use 400 instead; be consistent)429 Too Many Requestsrate limited; add Retry-After Making POST safe to retry A client sends POST /payments, the connection drops, and it does not know whether the payment happened. If it retries blindly it may charge twice. The standard remedy is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique value per intended operation and sends it in a header such as Idempotency-Key. The server stores the first result under that key and returns the stored result for any repeat: Calling pay("k1", 50) twice returns the identical response both times and charges ends at 50. A production version stores keys in the database in the same transaction as the charge, expires them after a day or so, and rejects a key reused with a different body.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Returning 200 for everything and putting the real outcome in the body. Clients, proxies, caches and monitoring all key off the status line, so a "200 with an error" is invisible to all of them. Verbs in URLs (POST /deleteUser) and everything tunnelled through POST.Changing state with GET, so a link prefetcher or crawler triggers deletions.PUT that behaves like PATCH, quietly keeping old fields when the contract said "replace".404 versus 403 confusion: sometimes you deliberately return 404 for resources the caller may not know exist, but do it on purpose.Retrying non-idempotent calls with no key.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Strict resource modelling gives a uniform, cacheable API but can fit awkwardly for actions and for reads that join many things. Pragmatic APIs mix both: resources for data, a few clearly named action endpoints for operations. What matters is that the exceptions are deliberate and documented.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Require idempotency keys on every endpoint that moves money or creates external side effects, and store them with the result. Return Location on 201, and Retry-After on 429 and 503. Document each endpoint's status codes, since clients write code against them.

title: Pagination, filtering and versioning

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: GET /orders on a table with ten million rows must not return ten million rows. An unbounded endpoint is slow, expensive and a ready-made denial of service. Every list needs a limit and a way to ask for the next part. And since the API will live longer than its first design, you also need a plan for changing it without breaking the code that already calls it. Bounded lists protect your servers, and a versioning policy protects your clients. Both are promises that are far cheaper to make at the start than to add later.
