sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Offset pagination ?limit=20&offset=40 maps to LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40. It is easy to build and lets a client jump to page 7. It has two problems. Cost: the database must walk past all 40 skipped rows to find the 41st. Page 50 000 does that walking every time. Consistency: the data moves between requests. Take ten rows, read three, delete row 2, then read the next three with offset 3: Offset page 2 returns [5, 6, 7]: row 4 shifted into the first page's range and was never shown. Keyset page 2 returns [4, 5, 6], which is right. Cursor (keyset) pagination Instead of "skip N", say "give me the rows after the last one I saw": WHERE id > :last ORDER BY id LIMIT 20. With an index on id the database jumps straight to that point, so page 50 000 costs the same as page 1, and inserts or deletes do not shift the window. The API returns an opaque cursor that the client sends back: Treat the cursor as opaque and validate it on the way back in: it is client input like any other (see the validation chapter), and encoding does not make it trustworthy. If you sort by something that is not unique (a timestamp), include a unique tie-breaker such as the id in both the sort and the cursor, otherwise rows with equal values are skipped or repeated. The cost: no jumping to "page 7", and a stable sort key is required. Filtering and sorting Accept filters as named query parameters (?status=open&created_after=2026-01-01) and sorting as an allow-listed field (?sort=-created_at). Never pass a client-supplied column name or ORDER BY fragment into SQL; map it from a fixed list instead. Always cap limit and apply a sensible default. Versioning A breaking change is one that makes a correct existing client fail: removing or renaming a field, changing a type or meaning, tightening validation, or adding a required input. Adding optional fields and new endpoints is not breaking, provided clients ignore fields they do not know. Common ways to carry a version: in the path (/v2/orders), in a header, or by date (a client pins "the API as of 2026-03-01"). Path versioning is the easiest to see, test and cache. Whatever you choose: Prefer additive evolution and keep one version alive as long as possible.Announce deprecation with a date, a Deprecation or Sunset header, and usage metrics per client.Never change the meaning of an existing field in place.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Paginating without a stable, unique sort order. Without it, two requests can disagree about which row comes next, so items repeat or vanish even with cursors. No maximum limit, so ?limit=1000000 works.Returning total counts on huge tables with COUNT(*) on every page; it can cost more than the page itself.Passing user input into ORDER BY or column names.Versioning everything at once, forcing clients to migrate for one changed endpoint.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Offset pagination suits small, slow-changing data and admin screens where jumping to a page matters. Cursor pagination suits feeds, large tables and anything under constant writes, at the price of no random page access. Many APIs offer cursors by default and keep offset only where a UI truly needs page numbers.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Default and cap limit, index the columns you filter and sort on, and make cursors opaque and signed or validated. Track which clients call which version so a deprecation is a measured decision, not a guess. Contract tests that compare responses against the published schema catch accidental breaking changes before they ship.

title: Inside a database: pages, the write-ahead log and row versions

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Disks and SSDs do not hand you one byte at a time; they move blocks. Memory is faster than disk by orders of magnitude, and power can fail at any instant. A database has to be fast and never lose a transaction it said was committed. Pages, a log and row versioning are the three ideas that make that possible. Almost every performance property you will study later (why scans are slow, why indexes help, why writes cost more than reads) follows from "data lives in pages, and the log is written first".

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Tables are heaps of pages A table is stored as a heap: a file divided into fixed-size pages (8192 bytes in PostgreSQL, checked with SHOW block_size). Each page holds many row versions, called tuples. You can see where a row lives with the hidden ctid column, which is (page number, slot within the page). On the lab table in this chapter's examples (one million rows of about 170 bytes): The whole table occupied 22 213 pages, about 174 MB. A query that must examine every row (a sequential scan) reads all of those pages. That number, not the row count alone, is the cost. Write-ahead logging Changing a page in memory and writing it back later is fast but unsafe: lose power in between and the change is gone. Writing every changed page to disk at commit would be safe but slow and scattered. The compromise is the write-ahead log (WAL): before a change is applied to data pages, a compact description of it is appended to a sequential log file. Commit returns only after the log record is flushed to durable storage (fsync). Data pages themselves can be written later, in the background. After a crash the database replays the log and recovers every committed change. Sequential appends are far cheaper than scattered page writes, so this gives durability at a small cost. You can watch the log grow: On the lab table, which had six indexes, one single-row insert advanced the log by 33 240 bytes. That is much larger than the row itself because the log also describes the index changes, and the first modification of a page after a checkpoint logs the whole page. It is a measurement from one run, not a constant. The same log is what replication ships to replicas, which a later chapter builds on. Row versions An UPDATE does not edit the old tuple. It writes a new tuple (possibly on another page) and marks the old one as no longer current: This is multi-version concurrency control (MVCC): each transaction sees the versions that were current when it started, so a reader does not wait for a writer. The price is dead tuples: old versions that nothing can see any more. Vacuum removes them and marks the space reusable; without it tables bloat and scans read pages full of garbage. The transactions chapter shows how MVCC produces the isolation levels.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Thinking DELETE or UPDATE immediately frees disk space. The old versions stay until vacuum runs, and the file does not shrink; the space is reused for future rows. Assuming a committed write is already in the data file. It is durable because of the log, not because the page was written.Disabling fsync or relying on a cache that lies for speed, which turns a crash into silent data loss.Ignoring table bloat on tables with heavy updates, then wondering why queries slow down.Estimating cost by row count instead of page count and access pattern.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Write-ahead logging makes every write do the work twice (log, then data page) and makes commit latency depend on the disk's flush time. In return you get crash safety and fast sequential I/O. MVCC removes read/write blocking but needs vacuum and extra space. Systems that tune these away (asynchronous commit, in-memory stores) get speed by accepting that a crash can lose recent data.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Watch commit latency and disk flush time, keep autovacuum healthy and monitor dead-tuple counts and table size, and take base backups plus archived WAL so you can restore to a point in time. Treat "the disk reports success" as a requirement: use storage whose flush semantics you trust.

title: Connections and connection pools

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Your app talks to the database over a connection: an authenticated session with its own state and, in PostgreSQL, its own server process using memory. Creating one takes several network round trips (TCP, TLS, authentication, session setup). Doing that for every request adds latency and wastes work; and the database only allows a limited number at once (max_connections defaults to 100 in PostgreSQL). A pool pays the connection cost once and turns "unlimited concurrent requests" into "a bounded number of concurrent queries plus a queue", which is something a database can survive.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: A pool owns up to max open connections. A request borrows one, runs its queries, and returns it. If none is free, the request waits in a queue until one is returned (or a timeout fires). Measured on a local PostgreSQL 16 with no TLS (so the real network cost is higher): Even with zero network distance, a fresh connection cost about 60 times more than reusing one. Across a real network with TLS the gap is larger. The queue Take a pool of max: 2 and six concurrent queries that each take 100 ms: The queries finished at about 105, 105, 207, 207, 309 and 309 ms: two at a time, three waves. That is the pool doing its job: the database never ran more than two at once, and the other four waited their turn instead of piling on. The hard limit Opening plain connections in a loop on the same server, the 101st was refused with sorry, too many clients already. With several app instances each holding a pool, instances × pool size must stay under the database's limit, with room left for admin tools and migrations. Sizing Start small. A common starting point is a pool of roughly the database's core count times a small factor (for example 2 to 4 times), then measure. Throughput usually rises and then flattens or falls as connections increase. If many instances need many connections, put an external pooler (such as PgBouncer) in front, which multiplexes thousands of client connections onto a few server connections. Note that session-level features (prepared statements, SET, advisory locks) can behave differently through a pooler in transaction mode.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Borrowing a connection and not returning it on an error path. Each leak shrinks the pool by one until every request waits forever. Always release in a finally block, or use helpers that do it for you. Holding a connection while doing slow non-database work (calling another API, waiting on a user).Pool size times instances above the database limit, which causes errors only at scale-out time.No acquisition timeout, so requests queue indefinitely instead of failing fast.Transactions left open, which pin a connection and can block vacuum.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: A small pool protects the database but makes requests queue during spikes, which shows up as latency. A large pool hides short spikes but can push the database into thrashing. You are choosing where the waiting happens: in your application's queue, where you can time out and shed load, or inside the database, where you cannot.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Export pool metrics (in use, idle, waiting) and alert on the waiting count, set a short acquire timeout, cap pool size per instance, and account for autoscaling in the total. Use a managed or external pooler when instance counts are large or short-lived (serverless functions especially).

title: gRPC and Protocol Buffers: typed service-to-service calls

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Between your own services you control both ends, so the flexibility of human-readable JSON buys less and costs bytes, parsing time and runtime type errors. A contract-first approach gives generated clients and servers in many languages, typed errors at build time and streaming. gRPC trades the browser-friendly, debug-by-eye simplicity of REST for strict contracts, efficient encoding and streaming between services you own.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The contract You describe messages and services in a .proto file; tools generate code for each language: The numbers (= 1) are field numbers: the identity of a field on the wire. What the bytes look like Encode {id: 150, name: "Ada", active: true, score: 300}. Each field is a key (field number and type), then the value. Integers use a varint: seven bits per byte, with the high bit saying "more bytes follow". 1 is 01, 150 is 96 01, 300 is ac 02. I computed those bytes by hand-encoding the format in a script; the protobuf documentation's encoding guide shows the same scheme. Here protobuf is 13 bytes against JSON's 49, about a quarter. Small numbers cost one byte, names cost none. The saving shrinks for text-heavy payloads and grows for number-heavy ones, and gzip narrows the gap for JSON. gRPC on top gRPC sends these messages over HTTP/2: many concurrent calls on one connection, header compression, and four call shapes: unary (one request, one response), server streaming, client streaming and bidirectional streaming. Calls carry deadlines that propagate downstream, and a defined set of status codes. Because of HTTP/2 framing and trailers, browsers cannot call gRPC directly; use gRPC-Web or a gateway, and keep REST/JSON for public APIs. Evolving a schema Add new fields with new numbers; old readers ignore unknown fields.Never reuse or renumber a field number; mark removed ones reserved.Do not change a field's type incompatibly.Treat missing fields as defaults, since protobuf3 does not tell "unset" from zero without the optional keyword. Run a compatibility check in CI so a breaking change fails the build.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Renumbering fields or reusing a deleted field's number. Old messages in queues or caches are then decoded as the wrong field, silently corrupting data. No deadline on calls, repeating the timeout mistakes from the fault-tolerance lessons.Exposing internal gRPC directly to browsers.Huge messages; stream or paginate instead.Treating zero as "missing" for numeric fields.Adopting gRPC for a two-service system where a plain HTTP call is simpler.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: gRPC gives strong contracts, smaller payloads and streaming; you pay with tooling, a build step, harder debugging (binary payloads) and no direct browser support. REST/JSON is easy to inspect and universal, at a cost in bytes and looser types. Many systems use REST at the edge and gRPC inside.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Set deadlines and retry policy per method, enable server reflection or keep protos in a shared repository, version services deliberately, propagate trace and request ids in metadata, and use a load balancer that understands HTTP/2 (long-lived connections defeat naive connection-level balancing).

title: Configuration, environments and secrets

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: The same build should run in your laptop, staging and production, behaving differently only because of configuration: database URL, ports, origins, feature switches, keys. Mixing these into code means rebuilding per environment and leaking secrets into version control, the most common way credentials escape. Code answers "what does the program do". Configuration answers "where and with what does it run". Keeping them apart lets one tested artifact move through environments unchanged.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Read once, validate at startup Read configuration from environment variables in a single module, validate types and ranges, and refuse to start on a bad value. A real example from this project's API (apps/api/src/config.ts) parses everything through a schema: Failing at boot with a precise message beats a mysterious error an hour later at 3 a.m. Note the coercion: environment variables are always strings, so numbers must be parsed (the A5 lesson on coercion applies). Defaults and layers Give safe defaults for local development, require production-critical values explicitly, and make dangerous values hard to set by accident (a production deploy should not silently use a development secret). Keep an .env.example documenting every variable with fake values; real .env files stay out of version control. Secrets are different A secret is configuration whose exposure causes harm: passwords, API keys, signing keys, tokens. Never in code, images or logs. Scan repositories and CI for leaks.Separate per environment so a leak of staging does not expose production.Least privilege: a key that can only do what the service needs.Rotate on a schedule and immediately on suspicion, which means the system must support changing a secret without a rebuild, and ideally two valid keys at once during rotation.Prefer a secret manager or the platform's encrypted secret store, injected at runtime, with an audit trail. If a secret leaks: revoke and rotate first, then investigate where it was used, then clean up history. Deleting the commit is not the fix. Feature flags and drift Feature flags are runtime configuration that turn behaviour on or off without a deploy; they let you ship code dark, ramp gradually and cut off a failing feature (the degrade-gracefully idea from fault tolerance). Treat them as debt: remove them when done. Drift is when environments diverge in undocumented ways, so "works in staging" means little. Define configuration declaratively, review changes like code, and keep staging structurally similar to production.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Committing a .env file "just for now". Public or private, a pushed secret must be treated as compromised and rotated. Reading process.env scattered through the code, so nothing validates it.Defaults that quietly work in production with dev credentials.Logging the whole configuration object at startup.One shared secret across environments and services.No rotation path, so after a leak a deploy of hours is needed.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Strict validation can block a boot over a typo, which is the point, but it needs good messages. Secret managers add a dependency and setup but give rotation and audit. Many feature flags give flexibility and a combinatorial test burden.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Inject secrets at runtime from a managed store, restrict who can read them, enable secret scanning in CI and push protection on the repository, document a rotation runbook, and rehearse it once so it works under pressure.

title: Tables, keys, constraints and joins

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Storing a customer's name inside every one of their orders repeats data and invites contradictions. The relational model's answer is to keep each kind of fact in its own table and refer between tables by key. The database then guarantees the references stay valid, and a query recombines the pieces when you need them together. Constraints turn rules ("an order belongs to a real customer", "a total is never negative") from hopes in application code into facts the database enforces for every writer.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The examples below run on PostgreSQL. A primary key uniquely identifies a row and cannot be NULL.A foreign key (REFERENCES) says this column must match a row in another table. Violating it fails: NOT NULL and CHECK reject bad values the same way (total = -1 fails with a check-constraint error). Joins An inner join returns only rows that match on both sides. A left join keeps every row from the left table and fills the right side with NULL when nothing matches. The result is Asha 2 orders / 120, Ben 1 / 20 and Chen 0 / 0. Chen appears because of the left join; with an inner join Chen, who has no orders, would vanish, and so would order 13, which has no customer. Counting o.id (not *) is what gives Chen a zero, because count(column) skips NULLs while count(*) counts rows. On the orders table, count(*) is 4 but count(customer_id) is 3. NULL means unknown SQL has three-valued logic: true, false and unknown. x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) can never be true, because "not equal to NULL" is unknown. The query for customers with no orders silently returned nothing. NOT EXISTS handles it correctly. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL to test for NULL.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Using NOT IN with a subquery that can return NULL. It returns no rows and raises no error, so the bug looks like "there is no data". Missing foreign keys "for performance", then cleaning up orphan rows forever.Inner join when you needed a left join, silently dropping rows with no match.Filtering the right table in WHERE after a left join, which turns it back into an inner join; put the condition in the ON clause.Joining without a proper condition, producing a cross product of every pair of rows.Using floating point for money; use integers of the smallest unit or numeric.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Constraints cost a little on every write and make some bulk loads and schema changes more careful. They buy correctness that no amount of application testing guarantees. Skip a constraint only when you have a specific, measured reason, and write down what you gave up.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Declare primary keys, foreign keys, NOT NULL and CHECK constraints in migrations, index foreign-key columns you join or delete by, and decide per foreign key what deleting a parent should do (restrict, cascade or set null) rather than taking the default by accident.

title: Normalisation and safe schema migrations

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Imagine an orders table that stores the customer's name and city in every row. Rename the customer and you must change every order; miss one and the data contradicts itself. Normalisation is the discipline of storing each fact in exactly one place. Normal forms are not exam trivia. They are a checklist for removing the three bugs that repeated data causes: update, insert and delete anomalies.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Anomalies Consider one wide table orders(order_id, customer_name, customer_city, item, price): Update anomaly: the customer moves, and you update three of their five rows. The table now claims two cities.Insert anomaly: you cannot record a customer until they place an order.Delete anomaly: deleting their only order also deletes everything you knew about them. The fix Move each repeated fact to the table that owns it and refer to it by key, as in the previous lesson: customers(id, name, city) and orders(id, customer_id, item, price). In practice, aim for these rules: every column depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key (roughly third normal form). The cost is a join to put the pieces back together. Denormalise deliberately and late. A stored order_count on the customer, or a copy of a price at the time of sale, can be right, but each one needs a clear owner and an update rule. A price captured on an order is not a copy in the bad sense; it is a historical fact that must not change when the product's price does. Migrations Schemas evolve. A migration is a numbered file of SQL (or generated SQL) applied in order, with the applied versions recorded in a table so each runs once: Rules that keep teams out of trouble: Never edit a migration that has run anywhere shared. Add a new one.Run them automatically and the same way in every environment.Keep them small, and know which statements take locks. Adding a column with a constant default is cheap in modern PostgreSQL, but changing a column's type or adding a constraint can rewrite or scan the table while blocking writes. Expand and contract To rename users.fullname to users.name without downtime, do not rename in one step, because old and new application versions run side by side during a deploy. Expand: add name (nullable). Deploy code that writes both columns.Backfill: copy existing values in small batches.Switch: deploy code that reads name.Contract: after nothing uses fullname, drop it in a later migration. Every step is safe to run, safe to roll back, and compatible with the previous app version.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Renaming or dropping a column in the same release that stops using it. During the rollout the old version still queries it and starts failing. Editing history: changing an old migration instead of adding a new one.A huge backfill in one transaction, which holds locks and bloats the table. Batch it.Adding NOT NULL or a foreign key to a big table without checking the locking behaviour first.No way back: shipping a destructive migration without a tested restore.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Normalised schemas protect correctness and make writes simple but need joins on reads. Denormalised ones read faster but push consistency work onto your code. Expand and contract trades speed for safety: a simple change becomes three or four deploys.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Run migrations as a separate, observable step before or during deploy, test them on a copy of production-sized data, set a lock timeout so a blocked migration fails instead of freezing traffic, and take a backup before destructive changes.

title: B-tree indexes: from a full scan to a handful of page reads

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Without an index, finding one user among a million means reading every page of the table and checking each row. That is the cost the pages lesson warned about. An index trades extra storage for a way to jump straight to the answer. For a competitive programmer: a B-tree index is a sorted structure with a huge fan-out. It is a balanced search tree designed so each node is one disk page, which makes the tree about three or four levels deep even for millions of rows.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: A B-tree keeps keys in sorted order inside pages. Each internal page holds hundreds of keys and pointers to child pages, so the tree is very shallow, and leaf pages point to the table rows. A lookup reads one page per level, so it costs O(log n) page reads with a large base, not O(n). Because leaves are sorted and linked, it also supports range queries, ORDER BY and prefix matches. Measured on one million users The users table had one million rows, 22 213 pages, 174 MB. Looking up one email: PlanExecution timeSequential scan (1 000 000 rows filtered out)about 98 msB-tree index scanabout 0.2 ms That is roughly 500 times faster on this machine, and the gap grows with the table. The price: the email index was 39 MB on disk, about a fifth of the table, and every insert, update of that column and delete must now maintain it too. Numbers are from one run on a laptop-class sandbox; the ratio is the lesson, not the milliseconds. When the index cannot help A function on the column (WHERE lower(email) = ...) cannot use an index on email; create an expression index on lower(email) instead (the lab had one, and the same lookup took about 0.1 ms). Selectivity matters too. WHERE country = 'IN' matched 200 001 of a million rows. Even with an index on country, the planner used a bitmap scan that still visited all 22 213 table pages and took about 123 ms. When a query returns a big fraction of the table, reading the whole thing in order is as good or better. Indexes pay off when they let you skip most of the data. Composite indexes An index on (country, created_at) is sorted by country first, then by time within each country. It serves WHERE country = 'IN' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10 by seeking to the country and walking backwards ten entries: about 0.03 ms in the lab, with no sort step. Column order matters: it helps filters on the leftmost columns, not the second column alone.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Creating an index and not checking that the query uses it. Always look at the plan; wrong column order, a function on the column or a type mismatch silently disables it. Indexing every column and paying for it on every write.Wrong order in a composite index so the leading column is never filtered.Indexing low-cardinality columns alone (a boolean, a status with three values).Forgetting foreign-key columns, so joins and cascading deletes scan the child table.Creating indexes on a busy production table without CONCURRENTLY, which blocks writes.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Reads get faster; writes get slower and storage grows. Each extra index adds work to every insert and to updates of its columns, and may block some optimisations. The right number of indexes is the smallest set that serves your measured queries.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on live tables, review unused indexes in the statistics views and drop them, and track slow queries with their plans. Re-check plans as data grows, because the best plan for a small table is often different from the best plan for a large one.

title: Reading EXPLAIN: how to see what the database actually does

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: "The query is slow" is not a diagnosis. The database already knows how it will run a query. EXPLAIN lets you look, so you can fix the actual cause instead of adding indexes at random. Performance work is a loop: observe the plan, form a hypothesis, change one thing, observe again. Without the plan you are guessing.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: A plan is a tree of operations, read from the innermost, most-indented node outwards. Each node shows how rows are produced, and with ANALYZE it reports actual time and rows. Read it: the database scanned the table, threw away a million rows and kept one. "Rows Removed by Filter" in the millions beside rows=1 is the signature of a missing index. After creating an index on email: Common nodes Seq Scan: read every page. Good when you need most rows.Index Scan: walk the index, fetch each matching row from the table.Bitmap Heap Scan: collect matching row locations from an index first, then read the pages in order. Used when many rows match, like the 200 001-row country filter, which still read all 22 213 pages.Joins: nested loop, hash join, merge join, chosen by the planner from size estimates. Add BUFFERS to see page hits (found in memory) and reads (from disk). Estimates versus reality The planner uses statistics about each table to guess row counts. When "estimated rows" and "actual rows" differ by orders of magnitude, the plan is probably wrong because the statistics are stale or the columns are correlated. ANALYZE tablename refreshes statistics (autovacuum normally does it). A safe loop Capture the slow query and run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on realistic data (a tiny dev table lies).Find the node with most of the time or the biggest estimate error.Change one thing: add an index, rewrite the predicate, refresh statistics.Run it again and compare. Keep the change only if the numbers improved.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on an UPDATE or DELETE in production. It executes the statement. Use BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE ...; ROLLBACK;. Tuning on tiny local data, where a scan is always the fastest plan.Reading only the total time instead of the node where it is spent.Ignoring estimate-versus-actual mismatches, the cheapest clue to a bad plan.Changing several things at once, so you cannot tell what helped.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: EXPLAIN ANALYZE gives the truth but costs a real execution and adds some measurement overhead; plain EXPLAIN is free but only an estimate. Forcing plans with planner settings can fix one query and hurt others, so use it to experiment, not as a permanent fix.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Enable slow-query logging and a statements-statistics extension to find the worst queries by total time, capture plans for them, and review after schema or data growth changes. Store the before and after numbers in the pull request that adds an index.

title: Transactions and ACID

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Moving money means two writes: subtract from one account, add to another. If the process dies between them, money vanishes. A transaction makes the pair indivisible: either both happen or neither does. The same idea protects any multi-step change, such as creating an order and decrementing stock. ACID is a contract between you and the database: you describe the unit of work, and it promises the unit is never half-applied, even with crashes and concurrent users.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The four guarantees: Atomicity: all statements apply, or none do. On error or ROLLBACK, the new row versions are simply never made visible.Consistency: a committed transaction leaves the database satisfying its constraints (keys, CHECK, foreign keys). The database enforces the declared rules; your business rules are consistent only if you declare them.Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work. How strongly is configurable; the next lesson covers the levels and what each allows.Durability: once COMMIT returns, the change survives a crash, because the log record was flushed first, as in the pages and WAL lesson. Mapping to mechanisms GuaranteeMostly implemented byAtomicityRow versioning, so uncommitted versions stay invisibleConsistencyConstraints checked at write or commit timeIsolationMVCC snapshots plus locksDurabilityWrite-ahead log flushed at commit In application code All statements must use the same connection, since a transaction belongs to one session. That is why you borrow one client from the pool rather than calling pool.query for each statement. Savepoints and deadlocks A savepoint lets you undo part of a transaction without abandoning it. A deadlock happens when two transactions each wait for a lock the other holds; PostgreSQL detects it and aborts one with an error. The standard defence is to always touch rows in the same order (for example, lowest account id first).

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Calling pool.query for each statement of a "transaction". Each call may use a different connection, so there is no transaction at all, and the BEGIN and COMMIT land on different sessions. Doing slow work inside a transaction (HTTP calls, user input), which holds locks and a connection.Never releasing the client after an error path.Ignoring the abort state after a failed statement.Retrying a non-idempotent side effect (an email, a payment call) inside a transaction that can be re-run.Assuming consistency without declaring the constraints that define it.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Longer transactions give wider guarantees but hold locks longer, reduce concurrency and bloat versions. Shorter transactions are faster and gentler but force you to design for partial progress. Keep the transaction as small as correctness allows, and make external side effects happen after commit.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Set statement and idle-in-transaction timeouts, log and alert on deadlocks and serialization failures, and retry the whole transaction (not just the failed statement) when the database reports a retryable conflict. Keep outbound calls outside the transaction, using patterns such as an outbox table.

title: Isolation levels, anomalies and lost updates

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Transactions running one after another are easy to reason about. Real systems run thousands at once, and running them truly one at a time would be too slow. Isolation levels are the dial between "safe like serial" and "fast with surprises". Most concurrency bugs in web backends are not exotic. They are check-then-act code (read a value, decide, write) running in two requests at once.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: PostgreSQL uses MVCC: each statement or transaction sees a snapshot of committed data. The level determines when the snapshot is taken. Read committed (default): each statement sees what was committed when it started.Repeatable read: the whole transaction sees the snapshot from its first statement.Serializable: behaves as if transactions ran one at a time; the database aborts any that would break that illusion. Everything below was run against PostgreSQL 16 with two sessions. Non-repeatable read Session A reads a balance of 100. Session B commits a change to 200. Session A reads again: Lost update Both sessions read 100, both compute 110 and write. The final balance should be 120 but is: Under repeatable read the database noticed and refused, so you can retry. Under the default level it quietly lost data. Two fixes avoid the problem at any level: An atomic update lets the database do the arithmetic under a row lock. FOR UPDATE locks the row after reading it so competing writers queue. Write skew Rule: at least one person must be on call. Alice and Bob are both on call. Each transaction checks "is more than one on call?", sees two, and takes themselves off. They touch different rows, so row locks do not conflict: Only serializable detected the invalid combination. Alternatives are to lock the rows you read (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the on-call set) or to enforce the rule with a constraint where possible. Retrying Serialization failures and deadlocks are normal at higher levels. The correct response is to retry the whole transaction from BEGIN, a bounded number of times with jitter, and only if its side effects are all inside the database.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Read-modify-write in application code under the default level: select the value, add in JavaScript, update. It works in tests and loses data under concurrency. Believing "I used a transaction" means "I am safe". Safety depends on the level and the access pattern.Using serializable without retry logic, so users see errors.Retrying only the failed statement rather than the whole transaction.Locking rows in inconsistent order, which causes deadlocks.Enforcing uniqueness by check-then-insert instead of a unique constraint.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Stronger isolation removes whole classes of bugs but increases aborts and coordination. Weaker isolation is cheaper but moves correctness into your code. A good default is read committed with atomic updates, unique constraints and targeted FOR UPDATE, using serializable for the few invariants that span several rows.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Prefer database-enforced rules (unique, foreign key, check) over application checks, make updates atomic expressions where possible, count and alert on serialization failures and deadlocks, and test concurrency with two parallel sessions or a load tool, not just unit tests.

title: NoSQL and data-model trade-offs

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Relational databases are general-purpose and strongly consistent, which is the right default (the B-chapters so far). But some workloads have a dominant access pattern or scale that a specialised store handles more simply: looking up a session by id at huge volume, storing nested documents read as a unit, or traversing relationships. "NoSQL" is a label for several different tools, not one technology. Pick the data store from how you will read and write the data, then check what it costs to operate and what consistency it gives. Fashion is not a requirement.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The families Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB used simply): get and set by key. Extremely fast and easy to scale; no queries beyond the key. Good for sessions, caches, counters.Document (MongoDB, Postgres JSONB): nested JSON-like records read and written as a unit. Good when the entity is naturally a tree and mostly accessed whole.Wide-column (Cassandra, Bigtable): rows partitioned by a key, with very high write throughput and queries that follow the partition design. Good for time series and event logs at scale.Graph (Neo4j): nodes and edges with fast traversal. Good for "friends of friends" and recommendation paths where joins would explode. Postgres can be a document store Postgres stores JSON as jsonb and can index it. On 300 000 events with a data jsonb column, finding events where data @> '{"type":"buy","user":42}': The table was 31 MB and the GIN index about 3 MB. So if you need flexible attributes next to transactional data, jsonb plus a GIN index often removes the reason for a second database. You keep transactions, joins and one backup story. What the schema looks like without a schema Nothing stops a writer from sending the wrong type: The insert succeeded. A report that adds up user ids now breaks on one row. With a document store, enforce shape in application validation (the A5 techniques), version your documents, and migrate old ones deliberately. Where the structure matters (money, inventory), keep those columns relational and put only the variable part in JSON. Consistency and joins Many NoSQL stores trade strong consistency, multi-row transactions or joins for scale and availability. That is a good deal when you can model around it (denormalise, one document per access pattern) and a bad one when your domain is relational. Design for the queries first: in a key-value or wide-column store the table layout is the query plan, and a new query shape can mean a new table or a migration.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Choosing a document store because the schema "might change", then discovering you need joins and transactions across collections. Relational databases handle schema change fine with migrations (B2). Using two databases when one would do, doubling operations and consistency problems.Modelling documents like tables and performing application-side joins.Unbounded arrays inside documents that grow until they hit size limits.Ignoring consistency settings and assuming a read sees the last write.Picking by benchmark headlines instead of your own access pattern.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: A specialised store can be simpler and faster for one pattern and loses the generality, joins and transactions of SQL. Every additional data store adds operations, backups, failure modes and a consistency boundary. The default should be Postgres, with an extra store added only when a measured need justifies it.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Decide ownership of each dataset (one system is the source of truth, the others are derived and rebuildable), validate document shapes on write, version documents, monitor store-specific signals (partition hot spots, replica lag), and rehearse restoring each store.

title: Caching with Redis: cache-aside, TTLs and eviction

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: A database query costs milliseconds and real work; reading a value from memory costs microseconds. If many requests ask for the same thing, computing it once and remembering the answer removes most of the load. A cache is a deliberate trade: speed and fewer database queries in exchange for possibly stale data and one more thing to operate. A cache is only worth having when the same data is read much more often than it changes. Measure that first; a cache in front of data nobody re-reads adds latency and complexity for nothing.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Cache-aside The application owns the logic. Read: look in the cache; on a hit return it; on a miss read the database, store the result in the cache with an expiry, return it. Write: change the database, then delete (or update) the cached entry. The hit rate (hits divided by requests) tells you whether it is working. Hit rate depends on the traffic Replaying 200 000 requests over 10 000 keys through a least-recently-used cache in a seeded simulation (Zipf-skewed traffic, where a few keys are much hotter than the rest): Cache capacity (of 10 000 keys)Hit rate1013.2%10039.2%1 00067.5%5 00088.6% Holding 1% of the keys already caught 39% of requests. With uniform traffic (every key equally likely), a cache of 1 000 keys hit only 9.9%, as arithmetic predicts. Skew is what makes caches work, so look at your real access pattern before sizing one. Eviction Memory is finite. On a real Redis 7.0 with maxmemory 2mb, writing 3 000 values of about 1 KB each: allkeys-lru: 973 keys remained and 2 050 were evicted. Writes kept succeeding.noeviction: after about 940 keys, writes failed with OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'. Common policies: LRU (drop the least recently used), LFU (least frequently used), volatile-* (only keys that have a TTL), random. Choose by what your data looks like, and decide deliberately whether Redis is a cache (evict) or a store (refuse). Time-to-live SET key value EX 2 expires the key after two seconds; reading it afterwards returned nil in the test. A TTL is your staleness budget: how long a reader may see an old value. It also bounds the damage of any missed invalidation.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Treating the cache as the source of truth. It can be flushed, evicted or restarted at any time; the application must work, only slower, with an empty cache. No TTL, so an invalidation bug serves wrong data forever.Caching per-user data under a shared key, leaking one user's data to another.Caching errors or empty results for too long.Counting on the cache for correctness (counters, locks) without atomic commands. Redis INCR is atomic; read-then-write in your code is not.No hit-rate metric, so nobody notices when the cache stops helping.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: More cache means fewer database reads but more memory cost and more staleness risk. A short TTL is safer and less effective; a long one is the reverse. Eviction trades completeness for a bounded memory footprint.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Export hit rate, evictions, memory use and latency; set an explicit maxmemory and policy; namespace and version keys (user:v2:42); and load-test with the cache empty, because that is the state after every restart and deploy.

title: Cache invalidation and stampedes

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: "There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things." The joke lasts because correctness depends on when a cached copy stops being allowed to answer. And caches create a failure mode that did not exist before: the load of a hot key's expiry. Every cache is a copy. Copies diverge. Your job is to decide how far they may drift, and what happens at the instant a popular copy disappears.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Write strategies Cache-aside with delete-on-write: update the database, delete the key. The next read refills it. Simple, and the usual default.Write-through: write to cache and database together. Reads are always warm, writes cost more, and the two writes can still fail separately.Write-behind: write to the cache and flush to the database later. Fast, but a crash can lose data. Rarely the right answer. The invalidation race Reader misses, reads the old row from the database.Writer updates the row and deletes the cache key.Reader stores the old row in the cache. Now the cache holds stale data and nothing will clear it until the TTL. This is why every cached entry should have a TTL, even when you also invalidate, and why correctness-critical reads (checking a balance before a payment) should go to the database. Stampede A popular key expires. In a test with 100 concurrent requests arriving while the key was missing, and a database call taking 50 ms: Single-flight (also called request coalescing) lets the first miss do the work and makes the others await the same promise: This works within one process. Across many instances use a short Redis lock (SET key lock NX PX 5000) or serve stale-while-revalidate: return the expired value immediately while one request refreshes it in the background. Jitter If a thousand keys are all cached with a 60-second TTL at startup, they all expire together. Add random jitter to each TTL (for example 60 s plus or minus 10 percent) so expiries spread out. When not to cache Skip caching data that changes constantly, is rarely re-read, must be exactly correct (balances, inventory at checkout), or is cheap to compute. First fix the slow query with an index; a cache that hides a missing index only postpones the problem.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Relying on invalidation alone with no TTL. One missed delete in an error path and the wrong value lives forever. Many keys with identical TTLs that expire in a burst.Cold-start outages: a deploy empties the cache and the database takes the full load. Warm it or ramp traffic.Caching a failure (a timeout stored as "not found").Caching authorization-sensitive responses without the user in the key.Using the cache as a lock or queue without understanding its failure modes.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Single-flight and locks protect the database but add latency for waiters and failure cases (what if the winner crashes?). Stale-while-revalidate gives smooth latency at the cost of briefly serving old data. Pick based on how stale each endpoint may be.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Alert on a hit-rate drop and on database load spikes that follow cache restarts. Put a short timeout on cache calls and fall back to the database, so a slow cache does not become an outage. Rehearse a cold cache in load tests.

title: Task queues and workers

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Sending an email, resizing an image or calling a slow partner API can take seconds and can fail. Doing it inside the HTTP request makes users wait and ties success to something outside your control. A queue accepts the work immediately ("I will do this") and workers do it in the background at their own pace. A queue converts a spike of requests into a steady stream of work, and turns "the partner is down" from a user-facing error into a delay.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The request handler inserts a job and returns. A pool of workers repeatedly claims a job, runs it, and marks it done. A job row needs a status, an attempt count and a time when it may next run: Claiming safely FOR UPDATE locks the chosen rows. SKIP LOCKED tells a second worker to skip rows another worker holds instead of waiting. Test with ten queued jobs and two workers claiming three each in separate transactions: Distinct jobs with no waiting. Without it, B stalls until A commits. Crashes and at-least-once A worker claimed jobs 1, 2 and 3 inside a transaction and its connection died before commit. Afterwards all ten jobs were queued again: the claim rolled back, so another worker will take them. That is the safety property, and also why a job can run twice: if the worker finished the side effect (sent the email) and then died before committing, the retry repeats it. The next lesson covers making that harmless. For long jobs, do not hold the transaction open for the whole run; mark the row running with a lease time, and have a reaper return jobs whose lease expired. Postgres or a broker? A Postgres queue is enough for modest volumes, needs no new infrastructure and lets you enqueue in the same transaction as your data change (the outbox pattern: no job without the row, no row without the job). Dedicated brokers (Redis-based queues, RabbitMQ, SQS, Kafka) scale further and offer features such as delays, priorities and fan-out; a later chapter covers Kafka.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Enqueuing a job after committing the database change in separate steps. If the process dies in between, the change exists and the job never will. Enqueue in the same transaction, or use an outbox. Workers that read then update in two steps, so two workers take one job.No limit on attempts, so a poison job retries forever.No dead-letter state for jobs that keep failing.Unbounded queue growth with no alert, until memory or disk runs out.Putting large payloads in the queue instead of an id to fetch.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Queues add delay (work is not done when the request returns), a new failure surface and the need for idempotent jobs. They buy resilience and smooth load. If the user needs the result immediately, a queue is the wrong tool; show a "processing" state or do the work inline.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Track queue depth, the age of the oldest job and processing rate; alert on age, not just depth. Run several workers, scale them on backlog, give each job a timeout, and keep a dead-letter list that a human reviews.

title: Retries, backoff and idempotent jobs

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Networks drop packets, services restart, and databases time out. A job that fails once will often succeed a moment later, so retrying is right. But retries are also a classic way to turn a small problem into an outage, and a way to charge a customer twice. Retries multiply load exactly when a system is weakest. They must be bounded, spread out in time and safe to repeat.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Exponential backoff Wait longer after each failure. With a base of 100 ms and a factor of 2 the waits are: Cap the delay (for example at 30 seconds) and the number of attempts. Jitter If a thousand workers fail together and all wait exactly 200 ms, they all retry together, producing a retry storm: synchronized waves that hit the recovering service at the same instant. Jitter randomises each wait (a common choice is a uniform random delay between zero and the computed backoff), spreading the retries over time. Idempotency An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as once. Setting a value is; adding to a counter is not. Techniques: Natural idempotency: UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE id = 7 is safe to repeat.Uniqueness constraint: record each processed event id in a table with a unique key; the second insert fails and you skip the work.Idempotency key: the client sends a unique key with the request; the server stores the key and the response and returns the stored response if the key repeats. (The REST chapter measured this pattern.) Put the dedupe insert and the database effects in the same transaction so they commit together. For effects outside your database (email, third-party API), pass the key to the provider if it supports one, or accept at-least-once and make the effect harmless. Poison jobs and dead letters Some jobs never succeed (bad payload, a bug). After a maximum number of attempts, move the job to a dead-letter state, keep its error, alert someone, and let operators replay it after a fix. Without this, one bad job can block or churn the queue forever. Know when to stop retrying Retry transient errors (timeouts, 503) but not permanent ones (400, validation failure). When a dependency is clearly down, a circuit breaker stops calling it for a while and fails fast, so you do not waste capacity.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Retrying at every layer: the client retries three times, the gateway three times and the worker three times, which multiplies into 27 calls for one failure. Retry at one chosen layer. No jitter, so retries stay synchronized.Retrying non-idempotent actions without a key.Retrying permanent errors forever.Infinite attempts and no dead-letter path.Ignoring the timeout of the retried call, so retries pile up while earlier attempts are still running.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Longer backoff protects the dependency but delays recovery for users. More attempts raise the success rate but also load and latency. Idempotency storage adds writes and a table to clean up; skipping it risks duplicate side effects.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Log each attempt with the job id and attempt number, track retry rate and dead-letter size as health signals, set per-dependency limits so one failing service cannot drain all workers, and test a dependency outage on purpose.

title: Full-text search: inverted indexes, stemming and ranking

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Users type words, not exact substrings, and expect plural forms, speed and sensible ordering. A B-tree answers "equals" and "starts with" well, but "contains the word cache" over millions of documents needs a different structure. An inverted index is the book-index idea: instead of document to words, store word to documents. Finding documents with a word becomes a lookup, the same trade as every index: space and write cost for fast reads.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The inverted index Given three documents, build a map from each normalised word to the ids of documents containing it: A query for cache AND lock intersects two sorted lists and gets document 3 without reading any document. Production indexes also store word positions (for phrases) and frequencies (for ranking). Normalising text Postgres turns text into a tsvector: tokens, stop words removed, stems applied. "The" and "were" vanished (stop words), "caches" became cach, and "running" became run, so the query for "run" and "cache" matched. The query text goes through the same pipeline, which is why the two sides agree. Choose the language configuration to match your text; the wrong stemmer gives odd results. Measured On 200 000 documents of about 12 words each (40 contain a rare word): Roughly 280 times faster for a rare term. For a very common word (160 000 of 200 000 documents contained cach), an index finds many rows and the gap shrinks, the same selectivity rule as B-trees. Ranking and its limits ts_rank scores documents by term frequency, so you can sort by relevance. It is basic. Search engines (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Meilisearch, Typesense) add stronger relevance models (BM25), typo tolerance, facets, highlighting, synonyms and distributed scaling. Use Postgres full-text for a few million documents and simple needs, and a search engine when relevance tuning, typo tolerance or scale demand it. A search engine becomes a derived data store: Postgres stays the source of truth and you keep the index in sync (via a queue, as in B7).

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Creating a GIN index on to_tsvector('english', body) and then querying with a different configuration or expression, so the planner cannot use it. Always check the plan. Using LIKE for natural-language search.Wrong language configuration, so stemming misbehaves.Searching user-typed text with to_tsquery, which errors on odd punctuation; use websearch_to_tsquery for user input.Letting the search index drift from the source with no rebuild path.Forgetting that indexes slow writes on frequently updated text.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Normalisation improves recall (more matches) at the price of precision (some surprising ones). A GIN index speeds reads and slows writes and uses space. An external search engine improves relevance and scale and adds an eventually consistent copy of your data to operate.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Keep a rebuild script for the index, measure query latency by term frequency, use websearch_to_tsquery for user input, debounce search-as-you-type, and test relevance with a small set of real queries and expected results.

title: Keeping a search index in sync with the source of truth

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Once search lives in its own engine, there are two copies of every searchable record. They will disagree: a deploy kills a worker, the engine is down for a minute, a bug skips one event type. A search that shows deleted items or misses new ones erodes trust quickly. Derived data needs a one-way flow from the source of truth plus a way to regenerate it from scratch. If you can always rebuild, drift is an inconvenience, not a disaster.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Three ways to feed the index Dual write: the request handler writes the database and then the search engine. Simple and wrong: a failure between the writes leaves them inconsistent with no record of what to repair.Transactional outbox: in the same database transaction as the change, insert an "index this record" row. A worker (B7) reads the outbox and updates the engine, retrying on failure. The change and the intent to index commit together or not at all.Periodic or on-demand reindex: a job rebuilds the index from the database. Slow for large data, but the ultimate safety net. Many systems combine 2 and 3: the outbox gives freshness, a nightly reindex corrects any drift. Larger systems use change data capture (reading the database's log, the same WAL from the first B-chapter) to feed indexes without application changes. Idempotent indexing Indexing "upsert document id 42 with this content" is naturally idempotent: doing it twice is harmless, which fits at-least-once delivery. Deleting an already-deleted document must not fail. Include a version (an updated_at or a counter) so a late, older event cannot overwrite a newer one. Living with a delay Seconds of lag are normal. Design the UI so it does not break: after a user creates an item, show it from the database response rather than expecting search to find it immediately; do not rely on search results for correctness (permissions must be enforced on the actual records, since an index can lag a revoked permission); and watch lag (age of the oldest unprocessed outbox row) as the health metric. Rebuilding safely Reindex into a new index, then switch an alias or pointer to it once complete, so users never see a half-built index. Keep the old one briefly in case you need to roll back.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Trusting the search index for authorization. A document a user lost access to can remain searchable until the index catches up. Filter results against the source of truth, or include permission data and update it with priority. Dual writes with no repair job.No lag metric, so a stalled worker goes unnoticed for days.Non-idempotent index updates, so retries duplicate documents.Reindexing in place, exposing partial results.Indexing sensitive fields that should never be searchable.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: An outbox adds a table and a worker but gives reliable, retryable propagation. Dual writes are simpler until the first failure. Full reindexing is robust and slow; incremental updates are fast and need careful handling of ordering and deletes.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Alert on outbox age and on the count of failed index operations, run a scheduled reconciliation that compares counts or checksums between the database and the index, keep reindex runnable on demand, and test by killing the worker mid-stream.

title: Timeouts, circuit breakers and failing fast

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Modern services call others: a database, a payment API, a recommendation service. The dangerous failure is not "down", it is "slow". Every request waits on the slow call; each waiting request holds a connection, memory and a worker; soon your service cannot answer anyone, and the failure spreads to its callers. This is a cascading failure. Reliability patterns are about containing damage: bound how long you wait, stop calling what is failing, and keep working in a degraded way when you can.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Timeouts A call with no timeout waits as long as the other side does. On a local test server that took two seconds to answer: Set a timeout on every outbound call: HTTP, database, cache and queue. Think of it as a budget: if your endpoint promises a response within 1 second and calls two services, their timeouts plus your own work must fit inside that second. Pass a deadline down the call chain so downstream services do not keep working after the caller has given up. Pick timeouts from observed latency (a bit above the 99th percentile), not guesses. Circuit breakers A breaker wraps calls to a dependency and has three states: Closed: calls pass through; failures are counted.Open: after too many failures, calls are rejected immediately without contacting the dependency.Half-open: after a cool-down, a few trial calls go through; success closes the circuit, failure reopens it. In a toy run, the dependency was down for 200 requests arriving at 100 per second, with a breaker opening after 5 consecutive failures and a 1-second cool-down: Instead of 200 slow, failing calls, the dependency saw 6 and the rest got an instant error the caller can handle. This is a model (single process, no concurrency), but it shows the effect: you spare the struggling service and your own threads. What to do when failing Fallback: return a cached or default value (a product list without recommendations). Mark degraded responses so clients know.Fail clearly: a fast 503 with Retry-After beats a hung request.Bulkheads: separate pools per dependency so one slow service cannot use all your connections, like watertight compartments.Load shedding: when overloaded, reject some requests early (lowest priority first) to keep the rest healthy. Together with backoff and idempotent retries (B7), these form the toolkit: timeout, retry with backoff, circuit breaker, fallback.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Using the library default timeout, which is often "none" or minutes. Check the default of every HTTP, database and queue client you use. Timeouts longer than the caller's own timeout, so work continues for a caller that already left.Retrying inside a tripped breaker and defeating it.One shared connection pool for fast and slow dependencies.A fallback that itself calls the failing service.No metrics on breaker state, so nobody knows features are degraded.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Short timeouts fail fast and may kill requests that would have succeeded; long ones waste capacity. Breakers protect systems and can stay open too long or open on a brief blip. Fallbacks keep the site up while hiding that something is wrong.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Export timeout counts, breaker state and fallback usage as metrics with alerts; test dependency failure and slowness (not only down) in staging; and review defaults of every client library when you add one.

title: Retry storms, overload and cascading failure

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Every defence in the previous lesson can be turned against you by its own arithmetic. A service at 100 percent of its capacity that receives retries is pushed beyond it, and then everything it serves gets slower or fails, which triggers more retries. Seeing the arithmetic is how you design against it. Outages are rarely one big failure. They are a small fault plus a feedback loop. Find the loops and cut them.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Amplification A dependency can handle 100 requests per second. Clients send 100 per second, and each failed request is retried up to 3 times with no delay. During an outage, every request fails and is retried, so the offered load is 1 original plus 3 retries each: Four times the load on the service that is failing. Layers multiply: a client with 3 retries calling a gateway with 3 retries calling a service with 3 retries can turn one user action into 27 calls (the B7 lesson on retries). Exponential backoff with jitter reduces the rate; a retry budget (allow retries only up to, say, 10 percent of normal traffic) bounds the total no matter how many requests fail. Overload and queues Little's law says concurrency equals throughput times latency. If latency rises because the service is saturated, concurrency (requests in flight) rises with it, consuming memory and connections. A queue in front adds delay: once the wait exceeds the client's timeout, the server is doing work nobody will read, and the useful throughput (goodput) falls toward zero. The system is busy and useless. Defences: Backpressure: tell producers to slow down (reject, return 429/503, shrink a window) rather than buffering forever.Bounded queues: choose a maximum size or maximum wait; beyond it, reject quickly.Load shedding: drop low-priority or newest requests early to protect the rest. Failing 20 percent fast beats failing 100 percent slowly.Deadlines: drop queued work whose caller has already timed out. Staying broken After the trigger is gone (a database restarted), a backlog and a retry wave can keep the service pinned above capacity. Recovery may need cutting traffic at the edge, shedding load, scaling out, or restarting with a cold cache protected by a ramp. This is why testing recovery, not only failure, matters. Degrade gracefully Decide in advance what to turn off when stressed: recommendations, analytics writes, non-essential features, expensive search. Keep the core path (login, checkout) alive. This is a design decision made before the incident, with feature flags to apply it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Adding more retries or longer queues to "make it more reliable". Both increase load on the failing part and delay the signal that something is wrong. Retries at several layers, multiplying attempts.Unbounded queues that hide overload until memory runs out.Health checks that restart overloaded servers, which adds a cold-start burst.Autoscaling that reacts slowly to a spike that has already caused a cascade.Never rehearsing an overload, so the first test is the real incident.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Shedding load deliberately fails some users to protect others, which is uncomfortable but better than failing everyone. Tight retry budgets reduce amplification and lower the success rate of transient errors. Choose limits from measured capacity.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Alert on retry rate, queue age and goodput (successful, on-time responses), keep a runbook for "cut traffic, shed load, then restore gradually", and run game days where you inject latency and failures into a staging copy and watch whether the defences hold.

title: Logs, metrics and traces

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: In production you cannot attach a debugger. When a user says "it was slow at 21:14", the only evidence is what the system recorded. Observability is designing that evidence in advance so that new questions can be answered without a new deploy. Three signals answer three questions. Metrics: is something wrong, and how badly? Traces: where is the time going? Logs: what exactly happened in this case?

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Logs: events with context Write structured logs: one JSON object per line with consistent fields, so tools can filter and aggregate. The request id is the key: generate or accept one at the edge, include it in every log line and pass it to downstream calls (this project's API echoes X-Request-Id and forwards it to the AI service), so one id joins everything a request touched across services. Use levels: error for things needing attention, warn for recoverable oddities, info for normal events, debug off by default. Never log passwords, tokens, full card numbers or whole request bodies; log identifiers, not content. Metrics: numbers over time A metric is a number sampled over time: counters (requests total), gauges (queue length, memory) and histograms (distribution of durations). Metrics are cheap to store and fast to alert on. The important lesson is what to summarise. For 10 000 request times where 2 percent were slow (800 to 1200 ms) and the rest were 20 to 40 ms, in a seeded example: The mean looks fine and the p50 and p95 look excellent, but p99 is a full second: one user in a hundred waits 33 times longer than the typical user. A user who makes many requests per page meets the tail often, so tail latency matters more than the average. Alert on p95 or p99, not the mean. What to measure: the RED method for request-driven services (Rate, Errors, Duration) and the USE method for resources (Utilisation, Saturation, Errors: CPU, memory, connection pool, queue depth). Traces: where did the time go A trace follows one request across services as a tree of spans, each with a start, a duration and attributes: the API span contains a database span and an HTTP span to another service. A waterfall view shows immediately that 380 of 400 ms were spent in one downstream call. Tracing requires passing a trace context (a header such as traceparent) along every call, and it is usually sampled (keep 1 percent of requests, plus all errors) to control cost. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for emitting all three signals.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Alerting on the average or on a single noisy log line. Alert on symptoms users feel (error rate, tail latency, saturation), not on every possible cause. No request id, so logs from one request cannot be joined.Logging at debug level in production, producing a flood and a bill.High-cardinality metric labels (a label per user id) that explode storage; use logs or traces for per-user detail.Logging secrets or personal data.Dashboards nobody looks at and alerts that always fire, which teach people to ignore alerts.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: More detail costs money and performance: verbose logs, more metric series and full tracing all add overhead and storage. Sample traces, keep metric labels low-cardinality, retain logs for a limited period, and spend the detail where decisions are made.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Write health and readiness endpoints that do not call heavy dependencies, define a few service-level objectives (for example, 99 percent of requests under 300 ms), alert on error budget burn rather than raw spikes, and make sure every on-call alert links to a runbook and to a dashboard filtered to the affected service.

title: SLOs, alerts and a method for debugging production

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Without a target you argue about whether the service is "fast enough" or "reliable enough" forever. Service-level objectives turn that into arithmetic, and a debugging method turns a 3 a.m. page into a sequence of steps instead of a panic. Reliability is a feature with a budget. An SLO says how much unreliability is acceptable, which is also how much risk you may take with new releases.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: SLI, SLO, error budget SLI (indicator): a measured ratio of good events to all events, such as "requests that return non-5xx within 300 ms".SLO (objective): the target for the SLI over a window, such as 99.5 percent over 28 days.Error budget: 100 percent minus the SLO. At 99.5 percent over 28 days, the budget is 0.5 percent of requests, or about 3.4 hours of total unavailability (28 days is 672 hours; 0.5 percent of that is 3.36 hours). When the budget is healthy, ship faster. When it is spent, slow down and invest in reliability. This is how the product and operations sides negotiate with numbers. Alerting that people respect Alert on symptoms users feel: error rate, latency percentiles, saturation approaching a limit, and burn rate (how fast the budget is being consumed: a fast burn pages, a slow burn opens a ticket). Do not page on causes ("CPU is 80 percent") unless they predict an imminent symptom. Each page needs a severity, an owner and a runbook link: what this alert means, how to check, and the first safe actions. If an alert fires and requires no action, delete or downgrade it. A debugging loop Scope: who and what is affected? One route, one region, one customer, everyone? Use metrics sliced by those dimensions.Compare: what changed? A deploy, a config change, a traffic spike, a dependency incident, an expired certificate. Check the deploy timeline first; most incidents follow a change.Hypothesise from the signals: errors up with latency up suggests a slow dependency; errors with flat latency suggests a bad deploy.Test cheaply: look at traces and logs for affected request ids; compare a failing and a succeeding request.Mitigate before you perfect: roll back, turn off a feature flag, shed load. Restore service first, find the root cause after.Verify the metric recovered, then write it up. Postmortems After a significant incident write a blameless postmortem: timeline, impact, root causes (plural; there is rarely one), what went well, what was lucky, and action items with owners and dates. Blameless means asking "what let this happen" rather than "who did it". Track the actions to completion, otherwise the document changes nothing.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Treating the postmortem action list as a wish list. Unowned, undated actions never happen and the same incident returns. Objectives set without looking at actual user needs or current performance.Paging on causes and getting woken for harmless events.No runbook, so every page is a fresh investigation.Fixing before mitigating, extending the outage.Skipping the postmortem for "small" incidents where the lessons are cheapest.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Tighter SLOs cost more engineering and slow feature work; looser ones accept more user pain. Sensitive alerts catch problems early and risk fatigue. The right setting is the one users and on-call engineers can live with, revisited each quarter.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Start with two or three SLOs (availability and latency of the main user journeys), burn-rate alerts with a fast and a slow window, a rotation with a handover note, a shared incident channel template, and a calendar slot to review action items.

title: Graceful shutdown: stopping without dropping requests

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: You deploy several times a day. Each deploy replaces running servers, and each old server may be in the middle of requests. Killing it drops those requests as errors the user sees. A graceful shutdown makes deploys, scale-downs and restarts invisible. Zero-downtime deploys are not a feature of the platform alone. The platform asks nicely; your process has to listen.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The sequence An orchestrator or process manager typically does this: (1) remove the instance from the load balancer (it stops being "ready"), (2) send SIGTERM, (3) wait up to a grace period (often 10 to 30 seconds), (4) send SIGKILL if the process is still running. Your job is to use the time between SIGTERM and SIGKILL well. On a test server that takes 1.5 seconds per request, with SIGTERM sent 0.4 seconds into a request: A minimal handler The order matters: stop accepting new connections, let in-flight requests finish, close idle keep-alive connections (otherwise close() can wait on them), then close resources such as database pools and queue connections, and finally exit with code 0. The timer is a safety net so a stuck request cannot block the deploy forever; set it a little below the platform's grace period. Readiness and the race The load balancer may keep sending requests for a moment after SIGTERM arrives. Handle it by making the readiness endpoint start failing immediately when shutdown begins, then waiting a short delay (a few seconds, matching the balancer's check interval) before closing the listener, so late requests are still served. A preStop sleep in Kubernetes serves the same purpose.
