Everything else that runs Background workers: stop claiming new jobs, finish or release the current one (B7: an unfinished claim returns to the queue by design), then exit.WebSockets and long-lived streams: send a close message so clients reconnect to another instance; reconnecting is part of the protocol.In-memory buffers (batched metrics, logs): flush before exit.Timers and intervals: clear them, or the event loop stays alive.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Handling SIGINT (Ctrl+C) in development but not SIGTERM, which is the signal production tools actually send. Shell wrapper as PID 1 that never forwards SIGTERM (see the signals lesson).Closing the database pool first, so in-flight requests fail on their next query.No deadline, so a hung request blocks the deploy.Idle keep-alive connections keeping close() pending.Exiting with code 0 after a forced timeout, hiding that shutdown was not clean.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: A longer grace period protects slow requests and slows every deploy. A shorter one speeds deploys and risks cutting work off. Choose it from the real distribution of request and job durations (the p99.9), not a default.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Test it: run a load generator during a deploy and verify no errors, log the start and end of shutdown with the number of in-flight requests, alert on exits with code 137 (killed after the grace period), and keep grace periods consistent between your app, the container runtime and the load balancer.

title: Injection, password storage and where trust ends

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: The A4 and A5 chapters established "never trust input". This lesson shows what that costs when ignored and the two fixes that matter most in practice. Security work is mostly closing a small number of well-known holes systematically. Each one below has a cheap, standard defence that you should apply without exception.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: SQL injection Building a query by gluing strings lets the input change the query's structure. Input ' OR '1'='1 against a lookup by name, on a table of three customers: The fix is to keep code and data separate: The driver sends the statement and the value separately, so the value is never parsed as SQL. Parameters cannot place identifiers (table or column names); for those, choose from an allow-list in code. ORMs and query builders parameterise by default, but a raw-SQL escape hatch with a template string reopens the hole. Storing passwords If your database leaks, the stored values decide whether passwords leak. Measured on one core of the sandbox: SchemeTime per hashGuesses per second per coreSHA-256about 0.0025 msabout 720 000scrypt (N=16384)about 38 msabout 32 That is a factor of about 20 000. A slow, memory-hard hash (scrypt, Argon2id, or bcrypt) makes each guess expensive. A unique random salt per password stops attackers precomputing tables and from cracking identical passwords together. Compare hashes with a constant-time function (crypto.timingSafeEqual), and re-hash on login if parameters are upgraded. Do not invent your own scheme. The trust boundary Everything that arrives over the network is attacker-controlled: body, headers, cookies, URL, even the User-Agent. Validate at the edge (A5), authorise every request on the server (A4), and never decide authority from client-supplied values such as isAdmin: true or a price in the request. Anything you send to the client (error messages, stack traces, ids) is also a disclosure decision. Least privilege The application's database role should not be a superuser. Give it only the rights it needs, use a separate role for migrations, keep secrets in the environment or a secret store (never in the repository), and scope API tokens narrowly. A compromised component should be able to do only what that component needed.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Logging full request bodies or tokens "for debugging". Logs spread widely and last long; secrets in logs are a common cause of real breaches. String-built SQL in one "temporary" admin query.Fast hashes or unsalted hashes for passwords.Returning detailed errors (SQL text, stack traces) to clients.Trusting hidden form fields or client-computed totals.One shared superuser database account for everything.Committing .env files or keys to version control.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Slow hashes cost CPU on every login and can be a denial-of-service lever if unprotected, so rate-limit logins and size the work factor to a login taking tens of milliseconds, not seconds. Strict least-privilege roles mean more setup and occasional permission errors, in exchange for a smaller blast radius.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Run dependency and secret scanning in CI, rotate credentials on a schedule and after any suspected exposure, keep separate credentials per environment, and test your login path under load with the real hash cost.

title: Rate limiting, abuse and the OWASP Top 10

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Even a correct, well-validated API can be hammered: a script guessing passwords, a client in a retry loop, a scraper. Limits keep one actor from consuming the shared capacity, and the Top 10 keeps you honest about the boring failures that cause most breaches. Defence in depth: validation stops bad input, authorisation stops bad actors, limits stop bad volume. Each layer assumes the others can fail.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The token bucket A bucket holds up to capacity tokens and refills at rate tokens per second. Each request takes one token; with none left the request is rejected with 429 Too Many Requests. This allows short bursts (up to the capacity) while enforcing an average rate. With rate 5 per second and capacity 10, firing 100 requests in one second (100 per second): 14 were allowed (the 10 in the bucket plus the roughly 4 it refilled), and 86 were rejected. The bound is capacity plus rate times time. Alternatives: a fixed window counter (simple, but allows double the limit across a window boundary) and a sliding window (smoother, a bit more state). Where state lives An in-process counter (the default in most rate-limit libraries) is per instance: with four instances behind a load balancer an attacker effectively gets four times the limit, and a restart resets it. For a real limit the state must be shared: a Redis INCR with an expiry is the classic, or a Postgres table when you want no extra infrastructure. A shared store must be fast and must decide what to do when it is down (fail open and risk abuse, or fail closed and risk an outage). What to key on Per user or API key (fair, and survives shared IPs), per IP (needed before login, but many users share one IP behind a NAT), and per endpoint (login and password-reset are far more sensitive than reading a list). Return Retry-After so well-behaved clients can slow down. The OWASP Top 10, as a checklist Broken access control: check the owner on every object access (the IDOR from A4). Most common.Cryptographic failures: TLS everywhere, slow password hashes, no secrets in URLs.Injection: parameterised queries, the previous lesson.Insecure design and misconfiguration: debug modes off, default credentials changed, minimal exposed surface, security headers.Vulnerable components: scan and update dependencies.Authentication failures: rate-limit logins, no user enumeration in error messages.Integrity failures and logging gaps: verify what you deploy, log security events.SSRF (server-side request forgery): when your server fetches a URL a user supplied, block internal addresses such as the cloud metadata endpoint.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Rate limiting only by IP behind a proxy without configuring trusted proxy headers: every request then appears to come from the proxy's address, so everyone shares one bucket, or the limit is trivially spoofed with an X-Forwarded-For header you should not trust. Limits only in the web app, not on the API behind it.Different error messages for "no such user" and "wrong password", which enables enumeration.Counting only failures so credential stuffing across many accounts slips through.Fail-open limiter that silently disables protection during an outage of the shared store.Forgetting expensive endpoints (search, export, AI) that need tighter limits.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Strict limits block abuse and also legitimate bursts (an office behind one IP). Shared state is accurate but adds a dependency and latency to every request; local limits are fast and approximate. Choose per endpoint and measure false positives.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Expose limit headers, monitor 429 rates by route and key, alert on sudden jumps in 401/403 and 429, keep an allow-list for trusted internal callers, and review the Top 10 against each service at design time and after major changes.

title: Reverse proxies and load balancing

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: One server has a capacity ceiling and is a single point of failure. Running several identical copies fixes both, but clients need one address and something must decide which copy handles each request. That something is a reverse proxy or load balancer. Load balancing turns "can this machine cope" into "how many machines do we add", provided your servers are stateless enough to be interchangeable.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: A reverse proxy accepts client connections and forwards requests to upstream servers. Typical jobs: terminate TLS once, route by host or path, compress, cache static responses, enforce limits, add request ids, and hide the internal topology. It adds a hop (a little latency) and becomes critical infrastructure itself, so it is usually run redundantly. Choosing a server Take three servers and 300 requests arriving every 15 ms. Most take 10 ms; about 5 percent take 400 ms (a heavy report, say). A seeded simulation of two policies: PolicyMean latencyWorst latencyRound robinabout 163 msabout 975 msLeast connectionsabout 51 msabout 510 ms Round robin sent requests to a server that was busy with a slow one while another sat idle. Least connections looked at what each server was doing right now. This is a simplified model (no network, perfect knowledge of load), so trust the direction, not the figures. Other policies: random with two choices ("power of two choices" gives most of the benefit cheaply), weighted (unequal servers), and IP-hash or cookie-based (stickiness). Health checks and draining The balancer probes each server (for example GET /healthz) and stops sending traffic to those that fail. Keep the health endpoint cheap and honest, and do not make it depend on the database or one DB outage removes every server at once. When deploying, drain: stop new requests to a server, let in-flight ones finish, then stop it. Sticky sessions versus stateless servers Sticky routing pins a client to one server so in-memory sessions work. It is a patch: load becomes uneven, and when that server dies the sessions die with it. Better: keep session state in a shared store (database or Redis) or in a signed token, so any server can handle any request. Layers An L4 balancer routes TCP connections without reading HTTP: very fast, less flexible. An L7 balancer parses HTTP, so it can route by path, header or cookie. A CDN is a geographically distributed set of caching reverse proxies for static and cacheable content, cutting latency by serving from near the user.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Putting per-user state in server memory and then adding sticky sessions "to make it work". It hides the design problem and turns every deploy into a mass logout. No health checks, so a dead server keeps receiving a share of traffic.Health checks that depend on every downstream service, causing cascading removals.Forgetting that the real client IP is in a forwarded header, breaking logs and rate limits.A single proxy instance, which is just a new single point of failure.Scaling the web tier while the single database stays the bottleneck.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: A proxy tier adds a hop, configuration and a component to secure and monitor; in return it gives redundancy, zero-downtime deploys and a place for cross-cutting rules. Smarter balancing needs more state (connection counts) and can still make mistakes when load information is stale.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Run at least two balancer instances, forward and trust client-IP headers only from your own proxies, set sensible timeouts and retry rules (retry only idempotent requests), watch per-server latency and error rates, and test taking one server away under load.

title: Replication, sharding and the limits of scaling

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Caches and indexes stretch one database a long way, but eventually reads outnumber what one machine can serve, availability demands a standby, or the data simply no longer fits. There are two basic moves: copy the data, or split it. Scaling data is harder than scaling stateless servers because data has to stay correct. Each technique trades some simplicity or consistency for capacity.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Replication One primary accepts writes and streams its write-ahead log (from the first chapter of this part) to one or more replicas, which apply it and can serve read-only queries. Benefits: read capacity grows with replicas, a replica can be promoted if the primary fails, and backups or analytics can run on a replica. Costs: with asynchronous replication a replica lags the primary, by milliseconds normally and far more under load. Consequences to design for: Read-your-writes: after a user saves something, read that user's data from the primary for a short while, or pass a position token.Stale reads are acceptable for feeds and dashboards, not for balance checks.Failover can lose the last few transactions if replication was asynchronous, and needs a mechanism to prevent two primaries ("split brain"). Replication does not increase write capacity: every write still goes to one primary. Sharding To scale writes and size, split rows across servers by a shard key (for example the user id). Each shard owns a slice. Costs: queries that cross shards are slow or impossible, joins and transactions across shards are hard, and resharding is painful. A poor key creates a hot shard (one celebrity user, or time-based keys sending all new writes to one shard). Which shard owns a key? Simplest: shard = hash(key) mod N. The problem is changing N. Moving from 4 to 5 servers with 10 000 keys: Consistent hashing places servers (many virtual points each) on a ring and assigns each key to the next server clockwise, so adding a server takes keys from its neighbours only. It is used by caches and distributed stores because rebalancing moves a minimum of data. The limits: Amdahl's law If a fraction p of the work can run in parallel, the speedup on n machines is 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n). At n = 8: p = 0.5 gives 1.78x, p = 0.9 gives 4.71x, p = 0.95 gives 5.93x. As n grows without bound, the speedup tops out at 1 / (1 - p): 2x, 10x, 20x. The serial part (a global lock, one coordinator, the primary database) caps everything. This is why finding and shrinking the serial bottleneck beats adding machines, and why "scale out" is not a magic word.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Reading from a replica right after a write and showing the user stale data. Route a user's reads to the primary briefly after they write, or design the UI to tolerate lag. Sharding too early, taking on large complexity for a problem an index would solve.Choosing a shard key with skew (country, date) and creating hot shards.Assuming replicas are backups. A bad DELETE replicates instantly; keep real backups.Mod-N hashing for a cache cluster, so adding a node invalidates most of the cache.Ignoring failover testing: a promotion procedure that was never rehearsed fails when needed.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Vertical scaling (a bigger machine) is the simplest and has a ceiling. Replication adds read capacity and availability with lag. Sharding adds write and storage capacity with large complexity. Choose the lightest option that covers the measured need.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Monitor replication lag and alert on it, rehearse failover, keep point-in-time backups independent of replicas, keep shard keys and routing logic in one place, and make resharding a planned, tested operation rather than an emergency.

title: Race conditions, locks and atomic operations

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Concurrency means several things in progress at once, whether on several cores (parallelism) or interleaved on one (the event loop). When they touch shared state, correctness depends on timing, and bugs appear only under load. This lesson makes the timing visible. Race conditions are the same bug in every layer: a read-modify-write on shared state, with a gap between the read and the write. You met it in the database (lost update) and meet it again in memory and in distributed systems.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Races without threads Measured: two deposits of 10 on a balance of 100 ended at 110. One thread, no parallelism, and still a lost update, because the await let the second call read the old value. Any code that reads, awaits and then writes shared state is exposed. Fix: do the update without awaiting in the middle, or serialise access with a lock. A lock (mutex) A mutex lets only one task into the critical section, the code that touches shared state, at a time. Others wait. With the lock, the same two deposits ended at 120. Always release in finally. Locks cost throughput (others wait) and, as the next lesson shows, can deadlock. Real threads: data races Worker threads can share memory through SharedArrayBuffer. Two workers each incremented a shared counter 1 000 000 times: The plain version lost about 28 percent of the increments: both threads read the same value and wrote back the same result. Atomics.add performs the read-modify-write as one indivisible step in hardware, so no update is lost and no lock is needed. The exact lost count varies from run to run; that variability is the signature of a race. CPU-bound work does speed up on real threads: a loop that took 337 ms on one worker took 195 ms split across two, a 1.73x speedup on a 2-core machine (not 2x: startup and scheduling cost). Choosing a tool Avoid sharing: give each worker its own data and combine results (message passing). The best fix is no shared mutable state.Atomic operations: for a single variable (counters, flags, compare-and-swap). Fast, no waiting, limited to simple updates.Locks: for protecting a multi-step invariant (move money between two accounts). Keep critical sections short, always release, and acquire multiple locks in a consistent order.The database: for state shared between processes, use atomic SQL updates, row locks and transactions (B4), not in-memory locks, which only work inside one process.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Check-then-act: if (!exists(id)) create(id) with an await in between. Two requests both pass the check and both create. Make the check and the action one atomic step (a unique constraint, an atomic upsert, a lock). Using an in-process lock to protect state that several server instances share.Forgetting to release a lock on an error path.Holding a lock across slow I/O, serialising your whole service."Fixing" a race with a sleep.Testing once and calling it correct: races are probabilistic; stress and repeat.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Locks are general but add waiting and deadlock risk. Atomics are fast and narrow. Message passing avoids shared state at the cost of copying and design effort. More parallelism gives speedup only for the parallel fraction of the work (Amdahl's law from the scaling chapter).

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Prefer database constraints and atomic statements for cross-request correctness, add timeouts to lock acquisition, test with concurrent load (many parallel requests against the same resource), and log lock wait time so contention shows up in your metrics.

title: Deadlocks, scheduling and worker models

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Once you have locks, you have a new failure that is not wrong answers but no answer at all. And once you know how to run things concurrently, you must decide how many workers and of what kind, which is mostly a question about whether the work waits on I/O or burns CPU. Locks fix races and create the possibility of deadlock. The skill is acquiring them in a way that cannot cycle, and keeping the amount of locked work small.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: A deadlock you can run Task T1 takes lock A then wants B. Task T2 takes lock B then wants A. In a test, each acquired its first lock, slept briefly, then asked for the second: Nothing crashed and no error was thrown: the tasks simply never finish. That silence is why deadlocks are dangerous. The four conditions A deadlock needs all four (the Coffman conditions): mutual exclusion (a lock is held exclusively), hold and wait (a task holds one lock while waiting for another), no pre-emption (locks are not taken away) and circular wait (a cycle of tasks each waiting for the next). Remove one and deadlock is impossible: Break circular wait with a global lock order (always A before B). This is the standard fix and it worked above.Break hold and wait by acquiring everything at once or not at all.Break no pre-emption with timeouts: give up and retry, as databases do by aborting one of a deadlocked pair.Avoid mutual exclusion with lock-free or message-passing designs. Producer-consumer Producers add items to a buffer; consumers take them. With a bounded buffer (capacity N), producers wait when it is full and consumers wait when it is empty. The bound is backpressure: a fast producer cannot overwhelm a slow consumer or exhaust memory. This is the in-memory version of the queues in the previous B-chapter and of the overload lesson: unbounded buffering just moves the failure later. Worker models Event loop (Node's main thread): one thread, many connections, ideal for I/O-bound work that mostly waits (the 0.3 chapter). A CPU-heavy handler blocks everyone.Thread pool for blocking calls (libuv runs file system, DNS lookups and some crypto off the main thread): a small default pool that can itself become a bottleneck.Worker threads: real parallelism for CPU work with message passing or shared memory. Splitting a loop across two workers ran 1.73x faster on two cores.Multiple processes (cluster, or several containers behind a balancer): isolation, use of all cores and resilience to a crash, with no shared memory; state moves to the database or cache. A rule of thumb: one event-loop process per core for I/O-heavy services, worker threads or a separate job service for CPU-heavy tasks, and measure.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Taking locks in different orders in different code paths. Each path looks fine alone; the cycle appears only when two run together. Calling unknown code (callbacks, network) while holding a lock.Unbounded queues between producer and consumer.CPU work on the event loop, stalling all requests.Spawning a thread per request, which exhausts memory under load.No timeout on lock or database waits, so a deadlock becomes a hung service.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Lock ordering is simple but needs discipline across a codebase. Timeouts recover from deadlock at the cost of retry logic. Processes isolate failures but share nothing, so coordination goes through slower external stores.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Monitor event-loop lag, pool wait times and queue lengths; add timeouts everywhere a task can wait; let the database detect and abort deadlocked transactions and retry them (B4); and test concurrency-sensitive paths with parallel load and, where possible, tools that explore interleavings.

title: Docker images, layers and the build cache

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: "It works on my machine" comes from differences in operating system packages, runtime versions and files. An image packages the application with everything it needs except the kernel, so the same artifact runs on a laptop, in CI and in production. An image is an immutable, versioned artifact. Deploying becomes "run image X" rather than "install things on a server and hope".

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Image, layers, container A Dockerfile is a recipe. Each instruction (FROM, COPY, RUN) produces a layer: a set of filesystem changes identified by a content hash. An image is a stack of layers plus metadata (the default command, environment). A container is a running process created from an image, with a thin writable layer on top that disappears when the container is removed. Images live in a registry and are referred to by name and tag, ideally pinned by digest. Containers are processes The kernel features that make this work: namespaces give the process its own view of process ids, network, mounts and hostname; cgroups limit CPU and memory. That is all. The process is visible from the host and can be killed from it, it shares the host kernel, and the isolation is weaker than a VM's. Consequences: don't run as root (0.4), and treat the container boundary as one layer of defence, not a vault. Layer order and the cache Docker reuses a cached layer if the instruction and its inputs are unchanged, and once one layer changes all later layers are rebuilt. So put what changes rarely first. This project's API Dockerfile (apps/api/Dockerfile) does it deliberately: If you change only source code, the install layer is reused and only the build re-runs. If you copied the whole repo before installing, every code edit would reinstall all dependencies. Use .dockerignore to keep node_modules, .git and secrets out of the build context. Multi-stage builds Build tools (compilers, dev dependencies) are not needed to run the app. A multi-stage build compiles in one stage and copies only the result into a small runtime stage: The final image is smaller, starts faster, and has a smaller attack surface. The CMD in exec form means no shell wrapper, so the graceful-shutdown handler from the earlier chapter actually receives the signal. Verification status: the sandbox this site was developed in has the Docker client but no running daemon, so the project's images were not built here. The Dockerfile reasoning above follows Docker's documentation; the first real build is the CI docker job. Check it yourself with docker build and docker history.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Putting secrets in the image (a COPY .env, an ARG token). Layers are inspectable and registries are shared. Inject secrets at run time. COPY . . before dependency install, defeating the cache.The latest tag, so builds are not reproducible.Running as root and shipping compilers and shells you do not need.Storing data in the container filesystem, which vanishes with the container; use volumes or external stores.One giant image for several services.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Containers give reproducible artifacts and dense hosting, and add a build pipeline, a registry and another layer to debug. Slim base images are small and lack debugging tools; full images are convenient and larger. Choose per service and keep a debug image or ephemeral debug container for incidents.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Pin base images by version or digest, scan images for known vulnerabilities in CI, set CPU and memory limits (a container over its memory limit is killed with exit code 137), add a HEALTHCHECK or readiness probe, tag images with the git commit, and keep images immutable: change by rebuilding, never by editing a running container.

title: Running containers: volumes, networking and Compose

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: A single container is a toy; real systems are an API, a database, a worker and a cache that must start in the right order, reach each other, keep data and be reproducible on every laptop. Compose captures that as a file. Containers are cattle, not pets: you can delete and recreate any of them. That only works if state, configuration and addresses live outside the container.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Where state lives A container's own filesystem is thrown away with the container. For data that must survive use a volume (managed by Docker, the right choice for database data) or a bind mount (a host folder, handy for source code in development). Configuration comes from environment variables (B11); logs go to standard output so the platform can collect them. Ports and networks Containers on the same user-defined network reach each other by service name: the API connects to db:5432, not localhost. A container's ports are private until you publish them: -p 8080:4000 maps host port 8080 to container port 4000. Publish only what must be reachable from outside; the database should be on the internal network only. Compose This project's docker-compose.yml describes the whole stack. The important idea is ordering by health, not by start: db is "healthy" only when it accepts connections; migrate runs once and must succeed; api starts only after that. docker compose up --build is then the whole system, and docker compose down -v removes containers and volumes for a clean slate. Verification status: as noted in the previous lesson, there was no Docker daemon in the development sandbox, so this file was checked by reasoning and by running each step by hand, not by docker compose up. If it fails on your machine, the logs below will say why, and a report helps fix it. Debugging containers docker compose ps and docker ps -a: state and exit codes (137 means killed, often out of memory or after the stop timeout; 143 means stopped by SIGTERM; 1 usually an application error).docker logs -f SERVICE: standard output and error.docker exec -it SERVICE sh: a shell inside a running container (slim images may lack tools).docker inspect: environment, mounts, networks, health status."Connection refused" between services: check the hostname (service name, not localhost), that the dependency is listening on 0.0.0.0 (not 127.0.0.1), and that both are on the same network.A container restarting in a loop: read the last logs before the restart; often a missing environment variable failing config validation, which is exactly the fail-fast behaviour you wanted.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Binding the server to 127.0.0.1 inside the container. It is then unreachable from outside the container even with the port published. Listen on 0.0.0.0. Using localhost to reach other services.Writing data inside the container and losing it on recreate.Publishing the database port to the world.Assuming depends_on means ready.A restart: always policy hiding a crash loop nobody looks at.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Compose is excellent for development and small single-host deployments and does not provide multi-host scheduling, rolling updates or self-healing at scale, which is what orchestrators such as Kubernetes add, with considerable complexity.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Treat Compose as a development and small-scale tool, keep volumes backed up (the restore drill applies), set resource limits, collect container logs centrally, and keep the same image from CI through staging to production, changing only environment configuration.

title: Kubernetes: scheduling, self-healing and rolling updates

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Once you have many containers on many machines, someone must decide where each runs, restart those that die, replace versions without downtime and give them stable addresses. Orchestrators automate this. Kubernetes is the dominant one. The core idea is a control loop: you declare the desired state ("3 replicas of image v2"), and controllers continuously compare it with reality and act to close the gap.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Verification status: there is no Kubernetes cluster in the development sandbox, so none of this lesson's behaviour was reproduced here. It follows the official documentation linked above; try it on a local cluster (kind or minikube) to see it happen. The objects Pod: one or more containers sharing a network and storage; the smallest schedulable unit. Pods are disposable and have changing IP addresses.Deployment: declares the desired number of identical pods and the image version; it creates a ReplicaSet that keeps that many alive.Service: a stable name and virtual IP that load-balances to the ready pods matching a label, so callers do not track pod addresses.Node: a machine in the cluster. The scheduler places each pod on a node that has the resources it requests; limits cap what it may use (exceeding memory gets it killed with 137, as in the Docker chapter).Ingress or gateway: routes external HTTP traffic to services.ConfigMap and Secret: configuration and sensitive values injected as environment variables or files (B11). Probes Readiness probe: is this pod ready for traffic? Failing pods are removed from the Service endpoints (it is the "not ready" signal from the graceful-shutdown lesson).Liveness probe: is it stuck beyond recovery? Failing pods are restarted. Keep it cheap and independent of dependencies, or a database blip restarts every pod at once.Startup probe: allows slow starts without liveness killing the pod. Rolling updates Changing the image in a Deployment starts a rollout: new pods start, and once ready, old pods are terminated, controlled by maxSurge and maxUnavailable. Terminating a pod runs the sequence from the graceful-shutdown lesson: removed from endpoints, SIGTERM, grace period, SIGKILL. If the new version never becomes ready, the rollout stalls and the old pods keep serving; kubectl rollout undo returns to the previous version. This is why readiness probes and graceful shutdown are what make deploys safe. Is it worth it? Kubernetes costs a learning curve, cluster operations (or a managed service's price) and a lot of YAML. It pays when you have many services, need autoscaling, multi-team self-service or portability. Alternatives: a platform-as-a-service, managed container services, or Compose on a VM.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Setting no resource requests and limits. The scheduler cannot place pods sensibly, one pod can starve its neighbours, and overloaded nodes evict pods unpredictably. Liveness probes that depend on the database.Skipping readiness probes, so rollouts send traffic to unready pods.Latest tags and no rollout history.Putting state in pods without persistent storage.Adopting Kubernetes for one service.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: You get declarative deploys, self-healing and a large ecosystem, and pay in complexity, cost and a new category of failure (misconfigured probes, resource limits, networking). The control loop is also eventually consistent: changes take seconds to propagate.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Use managed control planes where possible, set requests, limits and probes for every workload, run at least two replicas across zones, protect rollouts with PodDisruptionBudgets, keep manifests in version control and apply them through CI, and test node and pod failure before relying on self-healing.

title: CI/CD: from commit to production

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Manual releases are slow, error-prone and rare, which makes each one bigger and riskier. A pipeline turns release into a repeatable, boring routine, so changes are small, frequent and easy to undo. Small changes shipped often are safer than big changes shipped rarely, because failures are easier to find, explain and revert.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Verification status: pipelines run on hosted runners that are not available in the development sandbox, so the workflow below was checked by reading and by running its individual commands locally, not by executing it on GitHub. The first push will be its first real run. Stages This project's own pipeline (.github/workflows/ci.yml) is a concrete example. On every push and pull request it runs independent jobs in parallel: Secret scan: fail if a credential pattern appears in the repository.Web: install from the frozen lockfile, run the content check (frontmatter, links, prerequisite cycles), typecheck, tests, build.API: typecheck, tests against a real Postgres service container, build and a migration deploy.AI service: install the Python package and run its tests.Audit: dependency advisories for both ecosystems (also on a weekly schedule, since advisories appear without commits).Docker: build every image, start the whole stack with Compose and run a smoke test against it. Order checks from fastest to slowest so failures return quickly, run independent jobs in parallel, cache dependencies, and keep the whole pipeline in minutes: a 30-minute pipeline is skipped or ignored. Build once, deploy many Build the artifact (a container image) once, tag it with the commit, and promote that exact artifact through staging to production, changing only configuration. Rebuilding per environment means production runs something no one tested. Artifacts are immutable; a fix is a new build. Deployment strategies Rolling: replace instances gradually (the Kubernetes default). Simple; old and new versions run together, so changes must be compatible (the expand and contract rule from B2).Blue-green: run the new version beside the old and switch traffic at once; rollback is a switch back. Needs double capacity.Canary: send a small share of traffic (say 1 to 5 percent) to the new version, compare error rate and latency with the old, then expand or abort. Best protection, needs good metrics.Feature flags separate deploying code from releasing a feature, so you can ship dark and enable gradually (B11). Migrations and secrets Run database migrations as an explicit pipeline step, backwards-compatible with the previous app version, since both run during a rollout. Keep secrets in the pipeline's secret store, scoped per environment, never printed in logs; pull requests from forks should not receive them. Protect the production deploy with required reviews and a short-lived credential.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Rebuilding the artifact for each environment, or "fixing" production by hand. The next deploy overwrites the fix and nobody knows what is actually running. Flaky tests that people retry until green, hiding real failures.Slow pipelines that developers bypass.Deploys with no rollback plan or no health gate.Migrations that break the previous version.Secrets echoed in build logs.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: More automation and checks catch more problems and make the pipeline slower and more complex to maintain. Canary and blue-green reduce risk and cost infrastructure and monitoring investment. Choose the lightest strategy that matches how bad a bad release is for your users.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Track the four delivery metrics (deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to restore), gate deploys on health checks, keep rollback one command away and rehearsed, and record which commit and image are running in every environment.

title: What to test: the pyramid, and tests that earn their keep

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: You change code with confidence only if something tells you quickly when you broke it. Tests are that alarm. A bad test suite is slow, flaky or asserts nothing, and people stop trusting it; a good one makes refactoring boring. Judge each test by the bug it would catch and the seconds it costs. The best suites catch most bugs in seconds.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The pyramid Unit tests: one function or module with no network or database. Very fast (thousands per second), precise failures. Best for pure logic: validation, parsing, calculations, state machines.Integration tests: several parts together with real dependencies, such as the HTTP layer plus a real database. Slower, but they catch what units cannot: wrong SQL, constraint behaviour, serialisation, middleware order.End-to-end tests: the deployed system through its real interface. Slowest and most brittle; keep a few for the critical journeys (sign up, pay). This repository follows that shape. Running its three suites in the sandbox: Most are fast, pure tests, and the API tests run against an actual Postgres so queries, constraints and migrations are exercised. The simulations are deterministic (the same seed gives the same steps), which is precisely what makes them testable. What to assert Test behaviour through the public interface, not private implementation, so refactoring does not break tests. Cover: the normal path;boundaries: empty, one, maximum, just over the limit;failure modes: invalid input (the A5 lessons), timeouts, duplicate requests, authorisation failures (a user reading another user's record must get 404 or 403);regressions: every bug fixed gets a test that failed before the fix. Testing with real dependencies An integration test that uses a real Postgres catches things a mock cannot: a typo in SQL, a missing unique constraint, a migration that does not run. Use a throwaway database per test run, reset state between tests, and run the same Postgres version as production. Use test doubles (fakes or stubs) for things you do not control or that cost money: payment providers, email, third-party APIs, and for slow or random behaviour such as clocks. Make code testable Pure functions with explicit inputs are trivially testable. Separate decisions (logic) from effects (I/O), inject dependencies (the controller-service-repository layering from A6), and take the clock and random numbers as parameters. Nondeterminism is the enemy: a seeded random generator and an injected clock make time-dependent logic repeatable. Flaky tests A test that sometimes fails without a code change is flaky. Typical causes: real clocks and sleeps, shared state between tests, order dependence, races, and network calls. Fix by controlling time, isolating state and waiting for conditions instead of sleeping. Do not retry-until-green: that teaches the team to ignore red.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Writing tests that restate the implementation (assert that function A called function B). They break on every refactor and catch nothing. Assert outcomes, not steps. No assertions, or only "does not throw".Mocking the database and shipping a broken query.Shared mutable state between tests, so order matters.Slow suites that nobody runs locally.Only happy paths, so the first real input breaks things.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: More tests give more safety and more maintenance and wait time. Higher-level tests are realistic and slow; lower-level ones are fast and miss integration bugs. Spend where failure is expensive (money, security, data loss) and keep the rest lean.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Run the fast suite on every save or commit and the full suite in CI before merge, track suite time and flaky failures as metrics, keep a small post-deploy smoke test against the live system, and treat a test that cannot fail as a bug.

title: Testing HTTP APIs, databases and failure paths

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: An API's contract is its behaviour over HTTP: status codes, bodies, headers, and what it does to the database. The most valuable tests drive it the same way a client would and check both the response and the stored result. Testing at the HTTP boundary exercises routing, validation, authentication, the handler, the query and serialisation together, which is where integration bugs live.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Anatomy of an API test Arrange known state, act by sending a request, assert on the response and the database, and leave nothing behind. The assertion on stored state matters: a handler that returns an error after partially writing would pass a status-only test. Isolation Truncate tables between tests (simple, fast enough for small schemas).Wrap each test in a transaction and roll it back (fast; does not work if the code under test opens its own transactions or connections).A fresh database per test file, created from migrations (strongest; slower). Whichever you choose, run migrations in the test setup so the schema under test is the real one, and use the same Postgres major version as production. Seed only what each test needs, using small factory helpers rather than a giant shared fixture. The paths people skip Authentication and authorisation: no token gives 401; a valid user requesting another user's resource gives 403 or 404, never the data. Test this for every route that takes an id.Validation: a table-driven test of bad inputs (missing field, wrong type, too long, extra field) against one schema, asserting the error shape.Idempotency and duplicates: send the same request with the same key twice and assert one effect; submit a duplicate unique value and assert a clean conflict (409), not a 500.Concurrency: fire several parallel requests at one resource and assert the invariant holds (the lost-update scenario from B4).Dependency failure: make the external call time out and assert a defined response and no corrupted state. Time, randomness and externals Inject a clock and use fake timers (vi.useFakeTimers()) so "expires in 15 minutes" tests run instantly and deterministically. Seed random generators. Replace third-party services with a fake that you control (return success, return a timeout) at the boundary of your code, keeping everything inside it real. A contract test checks that your fake still matches the real provider's behaviour, run occasionally against the real service. Security and regression tests Add tests for the vulnerabilities you have closed: the injection string returns no rows, the forged cookie is rejected, the malformed header does not crash the server (this project has a regression test for a malformed Referer that once caused a 500). A fixed bug without a test comes back.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Asserting only the status code. Also check the body shape and the database effect, or a wrong-but-successful response passes. Tests that depend on execution order or previous tests' data.Real network calls to third parties in the main suite.Time-based sleeps instead of fake timers or condition waits.Testing the happy path only, especially for authorisation.A test database that differs from production (SQLite in tests, Postgres in production).

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Real databases make tests slower and more truthful; truncation is quick and transaction rollback quicker but less general. Fakes give control and can drift from the real service, so contract tests keep them honest.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Run integration tests in CI against the same database version you deploy, keep a post-deploy smoke test against the live URL, fail the build on any test that touches the public internet, and review failing-test history to find flaky or order-dependent tests.

title: Message brokers: logs, partitions and offsets

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: The queue in B7 hands each job to one worker and forgets it. Many systems need more: several independent consumers (billing, search, analytics) all reading the same events, the ability to replay history after a bug, and throughput beyond one database table. A log-based broker stores events durably and lets each reader move at its own pace. A log turns "messages in flight" into "a history you can read from any position". Consumers become simple: remember how far you got.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Verification status: Kafka was not available in the development sandbox. The semantics below are from Kafka's documentation, and the behaviour shown in the example comes from a small in-memory model I wrote to demonstrate the rules (partition by key hash, per-partition offsets, commit after processing). It is a model of the semantics, not Kafka itself. The log A topic is split into partitions, each an append-only sequence where every record has a numeric offset. Records are not deleted when read; they are kept for a retention period (or size), so any consumer can read from any offset and replay history. Partitions are spread across brokers for capacity and replicated for durability. Keys, partitions and ordering The producer chooses the partition, usually by hashing a key (a user id, an order id). Same key, same partition, so those records stay in order. In the model, with three partitions and keys u1, u2, u3 sending six events: Two lessons from one output. Ordering per key held. And the load was badly uneven (1, 0 and 5 events) because there were only three keys: a hot partition limits throughput, so choose a key with many distinct, evenly used values. Consumer groups Consumers in a group divide the partitions among themselves: each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group, so parallelism is capped by the partition count (10 consumers on 3 partitions leaves 7 idle). Different groups each get every record independently. Each group stores its committed offset per partition (in Kafka, in an internal topic). Offsets and delivery guarantees The order of "process" and "commit" decides the guarantee: Process then commit: a crash between them re-delivers the message: at least once (duplicates).Commit then process: a crash loses the message: at most once.Exactly once needs transactions that make the output and the offset commit atomic, or idempotent consumers. In practice: use at-least-once and make processing idempotent (B7, B9). Model run with a crash after processing the third message but before committing it: Lag Consumer lag is the distance between the latest offset in a partition and the group's committed offset. Growing lag means consumers cannot keep up; it is the key health metric and the broker-world version of queue age.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Assuming global ordering across a topic. If order matters, key by the entity whose events must be ordered, and accept that different keys are unordered. Too few partitions, capping parallelism, or too many, adding overhead; changing the count later changes key placement.Skewed keys creating a hot partition.Auto-committing offsets before processing finishes.Non-idempotent consumers under at-least-once delivery.Using a broker where a Postgres table queue would do.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Logs give replay, fan-out to many consumers and very high throughput. They cost operational complexity (a cluster to run and monitor), ordering only per partition, and eventual consistency between producer and consumer. For simple background jobs, the B7 queue is easier.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Alert on consumer lag and on rebalances, size partitions for the throughput you need at your target consumer count, set retention to cover your longest outage plus replay needs, define a dead-letter topic for poison messages, and test consumer restarts and rebalances under load.

title: Event-driven design: commands, events and keeping consumers safe

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: When an order is placed, many things should happen: charge, reserve stock, email, update search, feed analytics. If the order service calls each one, it must know them all and fail when any is down. Publishing one fact, "OrderPlaced", lets each interested service react independently. Events decouple who happened from who cares. The price is that you now design for delay, duplicates and change.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Commands versus events A command asks a specific service to do something ("ReserveStock"); it can be rejected, and the sender cares about the result. An event states something that already happened ("OrderPlaced"); it cannot be rejected and the publisher does not know or care who listens. Name events in the past tense, make them immutable facts, and include the id of the entity, a unique event id, a timestamp and a schema version. Put enough in the event for consumers to act, or the id to look it up; avoid huge payloads and anything secret. Publishing reliably Saving the order and publishing the event are two operations. Do not do a dual write (B8): use the transactional outbox. Insert the event into an outbox table in the same transaction as the order; a relay publishes rows to the broker and marks them sent, retrying on failure. Together with at-least-once delivery, consumers will see duplicates. Safe consumers Idempotent: record handled event ids (the unique-key technique from B7) so a replay changes nothing.Tolerant of reordering: events for different keys can interleave and a retry can arrive late. Use versions or timestamps so an older "ProfileUpdated" cannot overwrite a newer one.Isolated failure: after bounded retries with backoff, send a poison message to a dead-letter queue for inspection instead of blocking the partition.Replayable: a consumer that can rebuild its state by replaying history is easy to fix after a bug (reset the offset and reprocess). Schemas change Treat event schemas as contracts: add optional fields, never remove or repurpose fields, version breaking changes, and keep old and new consumers working during a rollout (the expand and contract idea again). A schema registry or contract tests catch violations before deploy. Flows across services A business process spanning services (place order, charge, reserve, ship) cannot use one database transaction. A saga is a sequence of local transactions where each step publishes an event, and a failure triggers compensating actions (refund, release stock). Sagas are eventually consistent and need careful design of what the user sees in the meantime ("payment pending"). Event sourcing goes further and stores the events as the source of truth; it is powerful and heavy, and rarely the right starting point.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Publishing events that are really disguised commands ("SendEmailNow"), recreating tight coupling with extra steps. Publish facts; let consumers decide what to do. Dual writes instead of an outbox.Non-idempotent consumers.Breaking schema changes without versions.Assuming ordering across keys.No visibility: no lag metrics, no dead-letter monitoring, no way to trace one business flow across services (propagate a correlation id).

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Events give extensibility and resilience to a downstream outage, and cost debuggability (flow is implicit), eventual consistency and operational overhead. A plain function call or a database transaction is often simpler within one service; use events at real service boundaries.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Carry a correlation id through every event, monitor lag and dead-letter counts, document each event as an API with an owner, test consumers against recorded events, and rehearse a replay.

title: WebSockets and real-time fan-out

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: HTTP lets the client ask; the server cannot speak first. Chat, live scores, collaborative editing and notifications need the server to push. Polling repeatedly wastes requests, and holding one connection open and sending when something happens is more efficient. Real-time features turn the server from a stateless function into something that holds state per connected client. That is what makes scaling them different.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The handshake A WebSocket starts as an ordinary HTTP request with Upgrade: websocket and a random Sec-WebSocket-Key. The server proves it understands the protocol by replying 101 Switching Protocols with Sec-WebSocket-Accept: the base64 of the SHA-1 of the key concatenated with a fixed GUID. I computed it for the example key in RFC 6455: After that the same TCP connection carries WebSocket frames in both directions. Use wss:// (TLS) so intermediaries cannot interfere. Frames are small A frame has a 2-byte header for payloads under 126 bytes (4 bytes up to 64 KB, 10 beyond), plus 4 bytes of masking key for client-to-server frames. A 20-byte message costs 22 bytes from server to client and 26 from client to server. A single HTTP polling request carries on the order of 137 bytes of request headers in a minimal example, before cookies and before any response headers. For frequent small messages the overhead gap is large. Alternatives Polling: the client asks every N seconds. Simple, cacheable, wasteful and laggy.Long polling: the server holds the request until there is data. Works everywhere, awkward at scale.Server-sent events (SSE): one-way server-to-client stream over plain HTTP with automatic reconnect. Often enough for notifications and feeds.WebSocket: two-way, lowest overhead; needs connection-aware infrastructure. Fan-out arithmetic Broadcasting a 100-byte message (plus a 2-byte header) to every connected client: The third row is about 0.8 Gbit/s from one broadcast channel and a million socket writes per second, more than one process handles. So you shard connections across servers, batch or coalesce messages (send the latest state every 100 ms instead of every change), and send only what each client subscribed to. Many servers A client is connected to one server, but the event may originate elsewhere. Use pub/sub between servers (Redis pub/sub, a broker): a server that receives a message publishes it, every server forwards it to the connected clients subscribed to that room. The load balancer must keep a connection on one server for its lifetime (not a problem for a single long-lived connection) and must allow long idle timeouts and graceful draining (shutdown: send a close frame so clients reconnect elsewhere). Reliability Send heartbeats (ping/pong) to detect dead peers and to keep proxies from closing idle connections. Clients reconnect with backoff and jitter (the retry-storm lesson applies: a server restart disconnects thousands at once) and resume from the last event id so no messages are lost. Apply backpressure: if a client cannot keep up, its send buffer grows; drop or coalesce messages, or disconnect it rather than exhausting memory. Authenticate at connect time and authorise every subscription (the IDOR rule applies to rooms).

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Trusting the connection once it is open. A user's permissions can change, and each message or subscription still needs an authorisation check. No heartbeat, so dead connections linger and memory leaks.Reconnect storms with no jitter after a deploy.Unbounded per-client buffers.Storing room state only in one process's memory and breaking with a second instance.Using WebSockets for something SSE or polling would do.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Open connections give low latency and low per-message overhead, at the cost of stateful servers, connection limits (file descriptors, memory) and harder deploys. Polling and SSE are stateless and simpler and use more bandwidth or lack the reverse channel.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Track concurrent connections, connect and disconnect rates, message rates and send-buffer size per server; raise file-descriptor limits (0.4); load test connection counts, not just request rates; drain connections gracefully on deploy; and cap message size and rate per client.

title: OpenAPI: the API contract as a machine-readable document

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: A client developer needs to know exactly what to send and what comes back, including errors. Prose in a wiki goes stale; a machine-readable contract can be tested, versioned and turned into code. The contract is the interface between teams. Making it a file that tools can read turns arguments about what the API does into a diff you can review.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Anatomy An OpenAPI 3.1 document is JSON or YAML with a few top-level parts: info and servers: name, version, base URLs.paths: each URL with its operations (get, post, ...), their parameters, request body schema and a response per status code.components: reusable pieces: schemas (JSON Schema), security schemes, shared responses.security: which operations need which scheme (a cookie, a bearer token, an API key). This project's API document (apps/api/src/openapi.ts, served at /api/openapi.json) describes 15 paths: health and readiness probes, the auth routes (register, login, logout, sessions, OAuth start and callback, account) and the progress routes. It declares a cookie security scheme and one shared Error schema, so every failure response has the same shape: { error: { code, message } }. One source of truth The same Zod schemas that validate requests at runtime are converted to JSON Schema for the document: Change a limit in the schema and the validation and the documentation change together. That is the pattern to aim for: schema first, with docs, types and validation derived. The alternative, contract first, writes the OpenAPI document by hand and generates server stubs and client types from it; it suits teams that agree on the interface before building, at the cost of keeping generation in the build. Why the error schema matters A documented, consistent error shape (a stable code for programs and a message for people) is part of the contract. Clients branch on code, never on message text (A5). Document each status an operation can return: 200, 201, 400 or 422 for validation, 401, 403, 404, 409, 429. What tooling reads it Docs UIs (Swagger UI, Redoc, Scalar) render it interactively.Client generators produce typed SDKs in many languages.Validators and mocks check traffic against the contract or serve fake responses before the backend exists.Contract tests (next lesson) confirm the running server matches the document.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: A document that lists only the happy path. Clients then discover errors, rate limits and auth rules in production. Describe failures as carefully as successes. Hand-maintained specs with no check against the server.Different error shapes per endpoint.Leaking internals (database field names, admin-only routes) into the public document.No operationIds, so generated clients have ugly method names.Treating the version string as decoration and never bumping it for breaking changes.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Schema-first generation keeps code and docs in sync with the least effort and ties the document's detail to what your schema library can express. Contract-first gives you design control and a review step before coding, and needs generation tooling and discipline to keep the implementation conforming.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Publish the document from CI as a build artifact, serve it at a stable URL, version it with the API, and keep internal and public documents separate so private routes are not advertised.

title: Contract tests, versioning and breaking changes

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: The contract document promises a shape. Servers change daily, and every change risks silently breaking a client you cannot see. Contract tests catch drift on your side, and discipline about compatibility protects the other side. You do not control when clients upgrade. An API change is a deploy that happens on other people's schedule, so compatibility is the default and breakage a deliberate, announced exception.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Testing conformance Drive the real app (as in the testing chapter) and validate each response body against the schema in the document for that status code. A contract test fails when a field is missing, has the wrong type, or when an undocumented status appears: This turns "the docs are right" from a hope into a failing test. If the document is generated from the same schemas, add tests for the parts that are not (error responses, headers, status codes). What breaks clients Compatible (additive) changes: adding an optional request field, adding a new response field, adding a new endpoint, adding an optional header. Breaking changes: removing or renaming a field, changing a type (number to string), making an optional field required, tightening validation (a shorter maximum length), changing the meaning of a value or a status code, removing an enum value, and changing error shapes. Treat a new enum value in a response as potentially breaking for strict clients, and document that clients must handle unknown values. Automated tools can diff two OpenAPI documents and flag breaking changes in CI, making the review explicit. Be tolerant, be strict The robustness principle for APIs: clients ignore fields they do not know (tolerant reader), and servers validate what they receive strictly (A5). If every client tolerates additions, you can evolve additively for years. Evolving without version numbers Add the new field alongside the old; keep both populated; announce the old as deprecated; measure who still uses it (log by client or key); remove it after a long, published notice. HTTP can carry the signal: a Deprecation header, a Sunset header with the removal date (RFC 8594) and a link to migration notes. When you must version Some changes cannot be additive. Options: a URL version (/v2/..., simple and visible), a header or date-based version pinned per client (as large payment APIs do, so each integration upgrades when ready), or a new resource name. Whatever you pick: define the support window, run old and new with shared code paths, and avoid more than two live versions.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Removing a "unused" field because the server logs show no reads. Clients that read it rarely or seasonally (a monthly report) will break later. Deprecate with a date first. Changing error codes that clients branch on.Tightening validation in a minor release.Silent behaviour changes under an unchanged schema (sorting, default page size).No usage data per version or client.Two versions with copy-pasted logic that diverge.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Strict compatibility keeps clients happy and accumulates legacy fields and code. Frequent clean breaks keep the API tidy and impose migration work on every consumer. Public APIs lean toward compatibility; internal APIs, where you control clients, can change faster with coordinated deploys.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Run an OpenAPI diff in CI that blocks breaking changes without an explicit override, log the client and version on every request, publish a changelog and deprecation policy, and send sunset headers and emails well before removal.

title: AI agents as backend workflows: loops, tools and failure handling

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Some tasks cannot be a fixed sequence because the next step depends on what was found: researching, triaging a ticket, fixing a failing build. An agent lets a model decide the next step. The model is not the hard part for a backend engineer; the machinery around it is. Treat the model as an unreliable component that proposes actions. Everything that makes other unreliable components safe (timeouts, validation, retries, limits, logs) applies unchanged.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Verification status: no model is called in this lesson's examples. They use a scripted stand-in for the model and a deliberately flaky tool, to show the loop control deterministically. They demonstrate backend behaviour, not model quality. The loop Send the model the task, the available tools (name, description, JSON Schema for arguments) and the history so far.The model either answers or requests a tool call with arguments.Your code validates the arguments, checks authorisation, runs the tool with a timeout, and captures the result or error.Append the result to the history and repeat from 1, until the model answers or a limit is hit. The model never executes anything. Your service does, with the privileges you give it. Failure handling Take a tool that times out twice before succeeding, and a loop with a step limit: Transient tool errors are ordinary; the loop needs a policy: retry with backoff for transient errors (B7), return the error text to the model for permanent ones so it can adapt, and stop after a limit. Always bound the loop: maximum steps, maximum wall time and a maximum token or cost budget. Without them a confused agent loops until your bill arrives. Why long loops get expensive Each step resends the whole growing history. If the context starts at 500 tokens and grows 400 tokens per step, the tokens processed by the model are 500 after one step, 6 500 after five and 23 000 after ten: roughly quadratic in the number of steps. Keep tool outputs short (summarise or truncate), keep step counts low, and cache stable prefixes where the provider supports it. Tools are API endpoints Validate arguments against the schema; never pass model output to a shell, SQL or file path unchecked (the injection lessons apply: a prompt injected via a web page can make the model request harmful calls).Least privilege: give each agent only the tools and data scope it needs, per user, enforced by your authorisation, not by the prompt.Idempotent or confirmable side effects: an agent may call "send email" twice after a retry. Use idempotency keys, and require human approval for irreversible actions.Audit log every call with the arguments, the result and who it ran for. Agent or workflow? If you can write the steps down, write them as ordinary code (a workflow), optionally calling a model for one step such as classification. It is cheaper, faster, testable and predictable. Use an agent only where the path really is open-ended, and keep a human in the loop for consequential decisions.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Putting security rules in the prompt ("never delete records"). A prompt is a request, not enforcement. Enforce permissions in the tool layer. No step, time or cost limit.Returning huge tool outputs that bloat the context.Non-idempotent tools retried after timeouts.Trusting tool output (a fetched web page) as instructions.No trace of what the agent did, so incidents cannot be reconstructed.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Agents handle open-ended tasks and add latency, cost, nondeterminism and a larger attack surface. Workflows are predictable and cheap and cannot adapt. Many products use a workflow with an agent only for the genuinely open part.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Record every run as a trace (steps, tool calls, tokens, cost, outcome), alert on loop-limit hits and tool error rates, run offline evaluations on a fixed task set before changing prompts or tools, and keep a kill switch.

title: RAG in production: retrieval, refusal and evaluation

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: A model alone does not know your product's documents and may invent. RAG feeds it relevant passages at question time, so answers can be grounded and cited. The engineering question is no longer "which model" but "did we find the right text, and do we know when we did not". This course's own tutor is a RAG system, deliberately without a generative model, which makes it a clean subject: every answer line must be a sentence from a cited lesson, so you can measure retrieval and refusal without any model noise.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: The pipeline Ingest: split documents into chunks (here: by lesson section and block type, keeping the heading path as context), store text, a keyword index and an embedding per chunk.Retrieve: for a question, run keyword search and vector search, then merge the rankings (reciprocal rank fusion) into one list.Gate: decide whether the retrieved text can support an answer at all.Answer: a generative model writes from the passages, or, as here, the system selects sentences directly (extractive), always with citations. Failures happen at each stage: bad chunks cut an idea in half, a poor retriever misses the right passage, a missing gate answers anyway, and a generator drifts away from the sources. Measure retrieval For labelled questions where you know which lesson holds the answer: recall@k: the right passage is within the top k.MRR: the average of 1 divided by the rank of the first correct result. On this project's held-out half (41 in-scope and 10 out-of-scope questions; the other half was used for tuning), measured in the sandbox with the zero-cost hashing embedder: Hybrid beat both ingredients. The vector row is weak because the embedder here is a dependency-free hashing model, which shares the lexical weakness without its precision; a real sentence-embedding model would likely lift it, but it could not be downloaded in the build environment, so that number is unmeasured. Say so rather than guess. The evidence gate Retrieval always returns something. A question about a tool the documents never mention still retrieves the closest passages. The gate asks whether the question's distinctive terms actually appear in them, weighting rare terms more than common ones, and requires the keyword or vector score to be high enough. On the held-out out-of-scope questions (many deliberately topic-adjacent: tools and ideas near the course topics but never taught), the hybrid refusal rate was 0.80 against an in-scope answer rate of 0.90. Weighting terms by rarity is what lifted refusal (measured on all 21 out-of-scope questions before the held-out split: 0.60 to 0.80). Those two numbers are the trade: raise the bar and you refuse more questions you could have answered. Some leaks remain: "What is a Kubernetes operator?" is answered because every word exists in the corpus even though the combination is uncovered. A lexical gate cannot see that; semantic models and answer-support checks can reduce it. Evaluation hygiene Write questions from the documents before looking at retrieval output, and include paraphrases that avoid the documents' vocabulary.Split into development and held-out halves. Tune thresholds on development; report results on the held-out half, which the tuning never saw.Include out-of-scope questions, since refusing correctly is half the job.Re-run when the corpus grows. Adding lessons changed the numbers: recall@3 slipped from 0.96 to 0.93 and an out-of-scope question started being answered. Evaluation is a regression test, not a one-time result.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Tuning the thresholds on all your questions and quoting the result. You have measured how well you fit those questions, not how well the system works. Chunks too large or too small, with no heading context.Only testing questions that have answers.Using a generative model without citations or without checking support.Changing several things between evaluations.Treating an evaluation set as fixed while the corpus changes.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: An extractive system is cheap, predictable and never invents, and reads less smoothly than generated prose. A generative layer reads better and can synthesise across passages, and adds cost, latency and a new failure mode (unsupported claims) that needs its own checks.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Version the corpus and embeddings, run the evaluation in CI with thresholds that fail the build on a regression, log (without personal text) the gate decision and retrieval scores, review refusals and unanswered questions regularly to find content gaps, and rate-limit the endpoint.

title: Production AI: cost, latency, safety and guardrails

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Once a feature calls a model, it inherits a new cost line, a new latency profile and a new class of security problems. Engineering it well looks like engineering any expensive, flaky dependency (B9), plus the problem that its output is text that someone may treat as trusted. Design as if the model will sometimes be slow, wrong or manipulated, because it will be, and decide what the system does then.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Cost and latency from first principles Cost is roughly (input tokens x input price + output tokens x output price) x requests. Do the arithmetic before building, with the current prices from your provider's page (they change, so keep them in configuration, not in your head). A worked shape with illustrative round numbers: if a request sends 3 000 input and 500 output tokens, and a million-token input price is P_in and output price P_out, then 100 000 requests per day cost 100 000 x (3 000 x P_in + 500 x P_out) / 1 000 000. The structure matters: input tokens dominate when you stuff retrieved passages and history into every call, so cutting context cuts cost and latency together. Latency is mostly output length: tokens are generated one after another, so a long answer takes proportionally long. Use streaming so users see text immediately, set a hard timeout, and keep outputs short where you can (ask for structured, concise results). Reducing both Cache identical requests (same input, deterministic settings) and use provider prompt caching for the large stable prefix (instructions, documents).Retrieve less, better: send the top few relevant passages, not everything.Route by difficulty: a small, cheap model for classification or extraction, a larger one only when needed.Batch offline work; accept asynchronous latency for non-interactive jobs.Rate-limit and budget per user and per day, so one user or a loop cannot spend the month's money (C3). Treat output as untrusted Never execute, render as HTML, interpolate into SQL or follow links from model output without the same handling as any user input. Ask for structured output (a JSON Schema) and validate it with your schema library (A5); on failure retry once or fall back. Constrain actions to an allow-list of operations. Filter or label content when the domain requires it, and cite sources so users can check. Prompt injection Prompt injection is when text the model reads (a user message, a web page, a document, an email) contains instructions that the model follows instead of yours. It cannot be fully prevented by wording. Layered defence: Least privilege: the model's tools can do only what the current user may do, enforced in code.Separate trust levels: mark retrieved or user-provided text as data, and never let it choose tools or targets by itself.Confirm consequential actions with the user or a human (sending, paying, deleting).Output checks: block responses that leak secrets or system text; scan for exfiltration patterns such as links containing data.Monitor and red-team: log attempts, and keep a test set of injection attacks that runs in CI. Fallbacks and people When the model is down, slow or over budget, degrade: cached answers, a simpler path, a message that says the feature is unavailable.
