For decisions that affect people (credit, hiring, moderation) keep a human accountable and provide a way to contest. Do not log sensitive prompts carelessly; they contain user data.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Sending the entire conversation and all retrieved text on every turn "to be safe". Cost and latency balloon, and irrelevant context can make answers worse. No timeout or budget, so one stuck call or loop is expensive.Rendering model output as HTML without sanitising.Giving the model broad credentials.Logging full prompts with personal data.Changing the model or prompt without re-running evaluations.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Larger models are more capable and slower and costlier. Caching and shorter contexts save money and add staleness and engineering. Strong guardrails reduce harm and false refusals annoy users; tune them with measured examples, not instinct.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Track tokens, cost, latency percentiles, error and refusal rates per feature and per user tier; alert on budget burn; keep prompts and models versioned with an evaluation run per change; and rehearse the provider being down.

title: Why distributed systems are hard: partial failure, time and quorums

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: A single process either works or crashes. A system of several machines can be half working: one node slow, a link dropped, a reply lost. Every later design chapter is a response to that. Distribution is chosen for capacity or availability, and it costs you certainty. Know what you pay.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Partial failure and the ambiguous timeout A client sends a payment request and the connection times out. Three worlds look identical: the request never arrived, it arrived and failed, or it succeeded and the reply was lost. You cannot tell from the client. So: make operations idempotent (B7), carry a key, and let the client retry safely. Quorums With N replicas, a write waits for W acknowledgements and a read asks R replicas. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one replica, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write (assuming a way to pick the newest). Checked by enumeration: Lower W or R gives lower latency and more availability, at the price of staleness. Logical time Vector clocks keep one counter per node. Compare two: if every entry of A is ≤ B's and one is smaller, A happened before B; if each is ahead somewhere, they are concurrent (a conflict to resolve). Computed: {A:2,B:1} vs {A:1,B:3} are concurrent; {A:1} vs {A:2,B:1} is before. Consistency and the trade-off During a network partition a system must choose: refuse some requests (consistency) or answer from possibly stale data (availability). That is CAP. PACELC adds that even without partitions you trade latency against consistency. Consensus protocols (Raft, Paxos) make a group agree on one order of operations, at the cost of coordination latency and needing a majority alive.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Using wall-clock timestamps to resolve conflicting writes ("last write wins"). With skewed clocks the older write can win and data is silently lost. Assuming the network is reliable or that latency is bounded.Retrying non-idempotent operations.Treating "eventually consistent" as "correct soon" without defining conflicts.Distributing before a single node is exhausted.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Strong consistency is simple to reason about and costs latency and availability. Weak consistency scales and pushes conflict handling onto the application.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Test failure, not success: kill nodes, delay and drop packets, and verify invariants afterwards. Measure replication lag and alert on it.

title: A method for system design: requirements, estimates and bottlenecks

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Without requirements and numbers, design discussions become opinions about technology. A method keeps the conversation on constraints. Most designs fail by solving the wrong problem or the wrong scale. Ten minutes of arithmetic prevents both.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Requirements. What must it do (functional)? How fast, available, durable, consistent (non-functional)? What is explicitly out of scope?Estimate. Daily users × actions per user ÷ 86 400 s = average requests per second; multiply by a peak factor (2–5×). Storage = records × size × retention. Bandwidth = QPS × payload.Sketch the simplest design (client, one service, one database) and find the first bottleneck against your numbers.Fix that bottleneck cheaply (index, cache, read replica, queue) and repeat.Write down trade-offs and failure modes. Worked: 10 million daily users, 5 actions each = 5×10⁷ per day ≈ 580 requests/s average, perhaps 2 000/s at peak. One tuned database handles that for reads from an index; the first bottleneck is more likely a hot query than raw volume. Keep the latency ladder in mind: memory reference ~100 ns, SSD read ~100 µs, same-datacentre round trip ~0.5 ms, cross-continent ~100+ ms (approximate, order of magnitude). A design that needs ten sequential cross-region calls cannot meet a 200 ms budget.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Starting with microservices, Kafka and Kubernetes before knowing the request rate. Skipping non-functional requirements.Ignoring peaks and skew (hot keys, celebrity users).Designing only the happy path.No stated assumptions, so nobody can challenge the numbers.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Simple designs are cheap to run and may need rework at scale; scalable designs are costly early. Choose by the growth you can credibly predict.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Revisit estimates against real metrics after launch and keep short decision records so later engineers know why.

title: Design: a URL shortener

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: A classic read-heavy design: write a long URL once, redirect to it many times. It shows capacity arithmetic, id generation, caching and abuse in one small system.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Requirements and numbers Create short link, redirect, optional expiry. Reads outnumber writes by perhaps 100:1; redirects must be fast and highly available. 100 million new links per month is ~40 writes/s; 100:1 reads is ~4 000 redirects/s. Code space Base62 (0-9, a-z, A-Z) gives 62ⁿ codes, measured: length 6 → 5.68×10¹⁰, 7 → 3.52×10¹², 8 → 2.18×10¹⁴. Seven characters is plenty for decades at this rate. Generating codes Counter then base62: a unique id (database sequence or a range handed to each app instance) encoded in base62: 125 → "21", 10⁹ → "15FTGg". No collisions; codes are guessable and sequential, which may leak volume. Mitigate by scrambling the id with a reversible permutation.Random: pick 7 random characters; insert; on unique-constraint violation, retry. Measured chance the next insert collides: 2.8×10⁻⁷ at 10⁶ stored, 2.8×10⁻⁶ at 10⁷, 2.8×10⁻⁵ at 10⁸. Cheap, rare retries.Hash of the URL: deterministic (same URL, same code) but truncation collides (13 collisions among 200 000 at 5 characters, expected about 19), so you still need a check. Storage and redirect One table: code (primary key), long URL, created, expiry, owner. Look up by primary key. Put a cache (B6) in front: hot links dominate. Use 302 if you want every click to reach you (analytics, edits), 301 when permanence and fewer requests matter; browsers cache 301 aggressively, so you cannot change the target later for those users. Abuse Validate URLs and block dangerous schemes, rate-limit creation (C3), scan for phishing, prevent open redirects to internal addresses (SSRF when you preview links), and provide takedown.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Assuming uniqueness without a database constraint, then serving the wrong destination after a collision. 301 for links you may need to change.No cache on a read-heavy path.Sequential ids that expose business volume.Unbounded creation by one client.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Counters avoid collisions and need coordination; random codes need no coordination and need retries; hashing deduplicates and still collides.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Track cache hit ratio, redirect latency percentiles and creation rate; keep expiry cleanup as a batch job.

title: Design: a distributed rate limiter

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Limits protect capacity and fairness (C3). On one instance it is a map; across many it is a shared-state problem. It is a small, sharp example of atomicity, shared state and failure policy.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Algorithms Fixed window: counter per client per time bucket. Cheap; bursts at the boundary (200 allowed in a short span in the measured run).Sliding window log: store timestamps; exact (100 allowed); memory grows with the limit.Sliding window counter: weight the previous and current window; approximate, small.Token bucket: tokens refill at a rate up to a capacity; each request spends one. Allows controlled bursts, steady rate. The usual choice. Sharing state Every instance must read-modify-write the same counter atomically, or two instances both see 99 and both allow. Options: a database row updated with UPDATE ... SET count = count + 1 ... RETURNING (atomic, uses what you already run), or Redis INCR with expiry (fast, extra infrastructure). This project's design choice is Postgres-backed state so no new service is needed; a test runs two app instances against one database and checks the limit is shared. Failure policy If the limiter store is down: fail-open (allow, risking overload) or fail-closed (reject, risking an outage caused by the limiter). Public APIs usually fail open for general limits and closed for security-critical ones such as login attempts. Responses Return 429 with Retry-After, and consider RateLimit headers so clients can back off (B7, B9). Key by user or API key where possible; IP alone penalises shared networks.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Read-then-write in two statements. Concurrent requests both pass the check. Trusting a spoofable forwarded IP header.No expiry on counters, so storage grows.One global limit with no per-route or per-tier limits.Not telling clients when to retry.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Exact algorithms cost memory or round trips; approximate ones are cheap and slightly lenient. A shared store adds latency and a dependency; local limits are fast and imprecise.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Track allowed versus rejected per route, alert on spikes, and test the store-down behaviour deliberately.

title: Design: a notification system

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Many events (signup, order shipped, password reset) must tell a user something, by channels with different speeds and failure modes. It combines queues (B7), events (D5), retries and preferences into one realistic system.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Trigger: a service records an event and enqueues a notification job (ideally with the outbox pattern, so the event and the job commit together).Worker loads the user's preferences, picks channel(s) and a template, and checks quiet hours and per-user rate limits.Send to the provider (email service, push gateway) with a deduplication key such as userId:eventId:channel. Store the key and result so a retried job does not send twice.Retry transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter (B7); after a limit, move to a dead-letter queue for inspection.Track status (queued, sent, delivered, failed, bounced) and handle provider callbacks and unsubscribes. Priority matters: password resets and security alerts use a fast queue; marketing digests use a slow, batched one, so a campaign cannot delay a login code. Scale: a campaign to 5 million users is a fan-out job; chunk it, rate-limit to the provider's quota and spread over time.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Retrying a send after a timeout without a dedup key. The first attempt may have succeeded, and the user gets two emails. Sending in the request path.One queue for urgent and bulk messages.Ignoring unsubscribe and bounce signals, damaging sender reputation.Putting secrets or full personal data in queue messages.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: At-least-once with dedup is simpler and robust; true exactly-once is rarely available end to end. Batching saves cost and delays delivery.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Alert on queue age and dead-letter growth, monitor provider error rates, keep templates versioned and test with a sandbox provider.

title: Design: a chat system

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Chat is the standard case for persistent connections, ordering and routing, building on the WebSocket lesson (D6). Users judge it by feel: instant delivery, no lost or duplicated messages, correct order.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Connect: clients hold a WebSocket to a gateway server (fall back to long polling where blocked). Gateways are stateful, each holding thousands of connections.Send: the client sends a message with a client-generated id. The server authorises it, assigns the conversation's next sequence number (a counter per conversation, in the database), persists it, then acknowledges the sender.Fan out: look up the conversation's members and which gateway each is connected to (a presence map in a shared store), then publish to those gateways via pub/sub; each pushes to its sockets.Offline users: they are not connected, so the stored message waits. On reconnect the client says "my last sequence number is 120" and the server replays everything after it, which also repairs any gap. Optionally trigger a push notification (F4).Duplicates: the client retries unacknowledged sends; the server de-duplicates by client message id. Ordering is per conversation, not global; a single sequencer per conversation (one writer) is simple and enough. For very large groups, fan-out cost grows with members (see F7); read receipts and typing indicators are ephemeral and need not be stored. Backpressure: a slow client cannot keep up; bound its outbound buffer and drop or disconnect it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Delivering to online users first and storing later. A crash between the two loses a message the sender thinks was sent. Ordering by client timestamps.No replay after reconnect.Unbounded per-connection buffers.Sticky load balancing assumed without a presence map.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Persist-then-deliver adds a write to the latency path and guarantees durability. Skipping storage lowers latency and loses messages on failure.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Monitor connection counts, delivery latency, reconnect rates and queue lag; roll out gateways with graceful drain (C2) so deploys do not drop everyone at once.

title: Design: file storage and sync

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: Files are big, uploads fail, and users edit them repeatedly. Treating a file as a list of chunks makes uploads resumable and syncs cheap. It shows why metadata and bytes are stored separately and how hashing gives deduplication for free.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Two stores Metadata (files, folders, owners, versions, the ordered list of chunk hashes) lives in a relational database (B2). Blobs (the chunk bytes) live in object storage, addressed by hash. Clients upload bytes directly to object storage with a presigned URL, so the app servers never carry the data. Chunking and dedup Compute SHA-256 per chunk; ask the server which hashes it already has; upload only the rest; then commit the file as an ordered hash list. Identical chunks, even across users, are stored once (mind privacy: cross-user dedup can leak whether a file exists). Fixed-size chunks are simple and fragile: insert 10 bytes at the start and every boundary moves, so measured reuse was 0 of 49. Content-defined chunking picks boundaries from a rolling hash of the content itself, so boundaries realign after the edit: 136 of 137 chunks reused. Cost: more CPU and variable chunk sizes. Resumable upload Track which chunks are committed; after a disconnect the client asks for the missing list and continues. Sync and conflicts Clients poll or subscribe to a change feed with a cursor. If two devices edit the same file offline, versions diverge (F0, vector clocks): keep both, e.g. a "conflicted copy", rather than silently overwriting. Housekeeping Reference-count chunks; delete only unreferenced ones after a grace period; verify hashes on read to catch corruption; encrypt at rest.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Deleting a chunk when one file drops it. Other files may reference it. Proxying uploads through app servers.No integrity check on download.Last-write-wins on conflicts.Tiny chunks, so metadata dominates.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Smaller chunks dedup better and add metadata and requests; larger chunks are cheap and re-upload more on edits.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Monitor storage growth, dedup ratio, orphan chunks and upload failure rates; test restore, not only backup.

title: Design: a news feed

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.text: The feed is the textbook trade between work at write time and work at read time, driven by skewed follower counts. One design question: where do you pay the cost of joining "posts" with "who follows whom"?

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Numbers Assume 10 million posts/day (~116 posts/s) and 200 followers on average. Fan-out on write: on each post, insert its id into each follower's feed list (a cache or table per user). 116 × 200 = 23 200 feed writes/s. A read is one lookup, very fast.Fan-out on read: store posts per author. A read fetches the latest posts from each of ~200 followed accounts and merges them: at about 231 feed reads/s each merges ~200 timelines. Writes are trivial, reads are heavier. The celebrity problem Follower counts are skewed. Writing one post to 50 million feeds is slow, bursty and wasteful (most followers are inactive). Hybrid: push for ordinary accounts, pull for very popular ones, and merge both when reading. Also skip pushing to inactive users, rebuilding their feed on return. Storage and paging Keep per-user feeds as a bounded list of post ids (the newest few hundred) in a cache, with posts fetched by id. Page with a cursor (last seen id or time), not offset, so new posts do not shift pages (B3 pagination). Deletions and blocks are applied at read time by filtering. Ranking Chronological is a sort. Ranked feeds score candidates with signals (recency, affinity, engagement), which adds a scoring stage and makes the result non-reproducible; keep it separate from retrieval.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Ignoring skew: a design verified with average follower counts collapses on the first account with millions. Offset pagination on a changing list.Unbounded feed lists.Fan-out inside the request path instead of a queue (F4).Forgetting deletes and privacy changes.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.text: Push gives fast reads and heavy, bursty writes; pull gives light writes and heavier reads; hybrid has the best behaviour and the most moving parts.

sections.heading: In production
sections.text: Monitor fan-out queue lag, feed read latency and cache hit rate, and set a follower threshold for switching strategy based on measurement.
